articles.title: JOL Reactivity in Deese-Roediger-McDermott Lists
articles.authors: Anthony Cruz; John Paul Minda
articles.abstract: Making judgments of learning (JOLs) during study often affects later test performance, a phenomenon called JOL reactivity (Double et al., 2018; Ingendahl et al., 2025). JOL reactivity has been observed across several word memory tasks. Some researchers have supposed that JOLs induce item-specific processing (Senkova & Otani, 2021), and others have supposed that JOLs induced relational processing (Chang & Brainerd, 2024). However, research on how JOLs impact false memory remains relatively limited. The goal of the present study was to characterize JOL reactivity in the Deese-Roediger-McDermott (DRM) false memory paradigm. In each experiment, participants studied intermixed DRM lists in either a JOL condition, a passive study condition, or a dual-task control condition. In the first experiment, JOLs enhanced correct recall relative to dual-task controls. However, JOLs had no significant impact on false recall in either experiment. Results were inconsistent with hypotheses that suppose JOLs encourage item-specific or relational processing.

articles.title: The Role of Working Memory in Reward-based Learning over Long Timeframes: Opponent Bootstrapping and Interference Effects of Working Memory on Incremental Learning
articles.authors: Yiwen Zhang; Xitong Chen; Benjamin Margolin Rottman; Anne Collins
articles.abstract: Learning from feedback is essential for effective decision-making in daily life. Previous experiments have indicated that feedback-based learning involves multiple processes, such as slower reinforcement learning (RL) and fast working memory (WM). However, most of these studies focused on the dynamics of RL and WM in short timeframes, ranging from a few seconds to minutes, whereas real-life learning may occur over hours, days, or weeks. This study aimed to investigate the interplay between RL and WM in long-term feedback-based learning. Instead of learning back-to-back iterations in quick succession, participants learned one or two iterations per day for 24 days. In this scenario, initial trials each day should isolate non WM decision processes, and WM should primarily assist in subsequent trials, and in low load conditions, for example when a given item was repeated in short succession. There were four key findings. First, WM contributed broadly to learning in trials 2-n of each day, especially in low load conditions, while trial 1 isolated non WM contributions. Second, when WM was available, it produced both immediate and long-term benefits. WM steered choices toward correct responses, allowing more immediate rewards, but also supporting the training of correct stimulus-action associations over time (a bootstrapping effect). Third, both test-phase performance and computational modeling revealed that using WM had an additional deleterious interference effect; trials during which WM was available produced slower RL updating and worse test-phase performance. Fourth, the long-term training benefits of WM overshadowed its interference effect, such that the overall effect of WM on long-term learning remained positive.

articles.title: A Longitudinal Investigation of Cannabis Use on Adolescent Neurocognitive Development in the ABCD Study®
articles.authors: Andrew Moore; Maria Perica; Rachel Visontay; Louise Mewton; Lindsay Squeglia
articles.abstract:
Objective. Evidence pertaining to the effect of adolescent cannabis use on neurocognitive development has been mixed, with recent reports highlighting the limitations of existing findings. By leveraging the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study® sample, the present study addresses previous methodological constraints to clarify cannabis’s potential effect on cognitive development.
Methods. Youth (N=4,191) performed neurocognitive tasks during their baseline (age ~10) and Year 6 (age ~16) follow-up assessments. Domains included overall cognitive function (crystallized/fluid), memory, executive functioning, processing speed, reward sensitivity, and language skills. Lifetime, cumulative cannabis use was divided along a median split to account for skewed data, resulting in no, low (≤5 cannabis use occasions; average=1.8), and high use (>5 use occasions; average=256) groups. Initial models (Bonferroni corrected, n=19) compared Year 6 follow-up cognitive performance between groups while controlling for baseline performance, sex, and age. Sensitivity analyses incorporated 1) socioeconomic status (SES), 2) additional substance use, and 3) SES and additional substance use.
Results. Cannabis use during early adolescence was significantly related (adj. p<0.05) to worse crystallized cognitive function (β=[-0.23,-0.21]), memory (β=[-0.35,-0.17]), and language skills (β=[-0.26,-0.13]). Cannabis effects remained generally consistent after controlling for SES alone. After controlling for additional substance use, the unique effect of cannabis use was no longer statistically significant.
Conclusions. The present study highlights that cannabis likely has an overall negative effect on neurocognitive development; while present over and above SES, this effect may not be substance specific. Future work aims to disentangle the shared effect of these relationships.

articles.title: puremoe: A PMID-Centered R Interface to PubMed and NIH/NLM Literature Data
articles.authors: Jason Timm
articles.abstract: Biomedical literature projects commonly begin in PubMed but require data from several additional National Institutes of Health and National Library of Medicine services. These services differ in their interfaces, response formats, batching rules, and data structures. The puremoe package provides a PMID-centered R interface for searching PubMed and retrieving article metadata, iCite metrics and citation links, PubTator3 annotations and relations, and open-access PubMed Central full text. It keeps remote retrieval explicit and provides source-specific local workflows for MeSH keyness, citation snowballing and network construction, and sentence-level context for biomedical entities and relations. We describe the package’s design, compare its scope with adjacent R clients, and demonstrate the workflow with a dated corpus on buprenorphine and opioid use disorder. puremoe is intended for moderately sized literature projects that require a structured NIH/NLM-centered corpus without maintaining separate API clients or a local literature index.

articles.title: Discourse prominent entities are not cognitively more prominent
articles.authors: Suet-Ying Lam; Shota Momma
articles.abstract: Four production experiments examined whether discourse prominent entities are more highly activated in memory. We developed an explicit information-processing model of how discourse prominence is hypothesized to affect planning speed at each stage of reference production, and tested its central prediction: that a pronoun referring to a more discourse prominent entity is planned faster than a pronoun referring to a less discourse prominent entity, when speakers are compelled to use a pronoun regardless of the discourse prominence of its antecedent due to Principle C. Contrary to this prediction, pronouns with antecedents introduced as subjects were not planned faster than pronouns with antecedents introduced as non-subjects. Instead, pronouns with antecedents introduced as the object of the preposition ‘by’ in passive sentences were planned faster than their subject counterparts. Two other potential sources of non-subject prominence, i.e., the informativity of an optional argument and its status as the source of information, also produced no planning advantage. These findings suggest that discourse prominence and level of activation in memory do not necessarily align, and therefore that discourse prominence should not be defined solely in terms of memory activation. We discuss a coherence-based alternative under which reference to an entity contributes to discourse coherence without necessarily facilitating its retrieval.

articles.title: Prebunking via Induction: Categorization Practice Reduces Misinformation Susceptibility
articles.authors: Benjamin Motz; Kendall Moore; Keven Gregg; Jon Roozenbeek
articles.abstract: Effective misinformation resistance requires practice, yet it has been unclear what this practice should ideally entail. In the current study, we compare a category induction strategy (practicing categorizing social media posts according to features of misinformation) with an active control reflecting standard educational practice (instruction about features of misinformation followed by formative assessments) in two 9th-grade honors civics classes. Students completed weekly learning activities as part of their routine classwork, and we used a shared educational research infrastructure (Terracotta) to randomly assign students to category induction or active control versions of these activities. Students assigned to inductive practice demonstrated advantages in identifying features of misinformation, with no deficit in conceptual knowledge about the manipulation techniques. And importantly, students assigned to inductive practice showed significantly better discrimination between real and fake news headlines on a novel transfer task using a completely different stimulus and task format. Furthermore, students in the category induction condition were less willing to share manipulative content and were more willing to share credible content, without becoming generally skeptical of online information. These results demonstrate the utility of category induction as an educational strategy, and reinforce the importance of authentic practice activities for developing effective misinformation resistance.

articles.title: LLM agents in online communities draw fewer replies and more disagreement when labeled as AI
articles.authors: Sara Major; Aleksandar Tomašević; Ana Vranić; Darja Cvetkovic; Dušan Vudragović; Boris Stupovski; Marija Mitrovic Dankulov
articles.abstract: Autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) accounts now post, reply, and vote alongside people in online communities. Visible identity labels may act as cultural markers that set these accounts apart from human participants. In a field experiment on YSocial, a Reddit-like platform, 36 students at a Serbian university discussed globally circulated popular culture in English alongside 72 AI accounts with persistent personas and relationship-specific memories over 21 experiment days. AI accounts were labeled in one community and unlabeled in the other. Among 2,143 human replies, the estimated probability of replying to an AI-authored post or comment was 3.5 percentage points higher under hidden labels, given the same eligible earlier thread contributions (95% credible interval 0.5–6.5). In browser telemetry, the disadvantage of AI-authored posts in direct thread entry from the feed was 4.4 percentage points smaller under hidden labels (95% credible interval 0.8–8.1). In both communities, participants were more likely to answer an AI account that had just replied to them. The gap in criticism, including polite disagreement, between replies to AI and human accounts was 13.3 percentage points larger in the visible-label community (95% credible interval 5.1–21.4), mainly criticism of content; the corresponding gap in downvotes from other participants was also larger there, and nearly all references to AI identity occurred there. Toxicity differences were uncertain. Visible labels were associated with less selection and more criticism of AI contributions.

articles.title: Beyond Symptom Reduction: Interconnectedness and Self-Transcendent Emotions During MDMA Sessions Predict Flourishing, Not Symptom Change, in Social Anxiety Disorder Treatment
articles.authors: Christina Chwyl; M. Kati Lear; Jason B Luoma
articles.abstract: By fostering certain self-transcendent experiences (STE)—those characterized by interconnectedness and other-oriented emotions—3,4-Methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA)-assisted therapy (MDMA-AT) has been hypothesized to disrupt social anxiety disorder maintenance processes, including negative self-focus, self-criticism, and isolation, thereby enhancing wellbeing. This secondary analysis used data from a randomized waitlist controlled trial of MDMA-AT for generalized social anxiety disorder (N = 20; NCT05138068). It characterized STE during MDMA-AT and examined their relationships with social anxiety symptoms and wellbeing outcomes. Participants reported on STE following two MDMA sessions. Outcomes (social anxiety, gratitude, belonging, purpose in life) were measured at baseline and post-treatment (16 weeks). Paired-samples t-tests examined changes across sessions and pre-to-post treatment, and regression analyses tested whether in-session experiences predicted outcome improvements. Sessions elicited blissful states, and positive and ST emotions, with few negative emotions reported. In-session experiences, especially connection-oriented STE, predicted greater post-treatment belonging, gratitude, and purpose in life, though not social anxiety reduction. STE involving a sense of self-loss were infrequently endorsed and did not predict outcomes. Findings highlight the potential importance of connection-focused STE and emotions during MDMA-AT for promoting psychological flourishing and eudaimonic wellbeing, laying the groundwork for future larger-scale mechanistic trials.

articles.title: Testing the Translational Validity of the Learned Helplessness Model in Humans: Effects of Stressor Controllability on Reward Processing and Social Functioning
articles.authors: Jean-Simon Fortin; Charles Parisien; Andréanne Richard-Robert; Norah Ho-El Abidi; Elina Khalaf; Catherine Parent; Mathilde Lafleur; Justine Le Blanc-Brillon; Xin Song; Soren Wainio-Theberge
articles.abstract: Learned helplessness (LH) theory proposes that uncontrollable stress, but not otherwise identical controllable stress, produces behavioral consequences relevant to depression. Although extensively validated in animal models, the extent to which experimentally induced uncontrollability in humans reproduces depression-related behavioral alterations remains unclear. Here, we conducted one of the largest experimental investigations of human LH to date, using a preregistered yoked-control design in which participants were exposed to identical aversive stimuli but differed in their ability to control stimulus termination. We first examined whether uncontrollability impaired performance on a classic LH outcome measure, the anagram task. We then assessed its effects across multiple depression-relevant domains, including reward learning, effort-based reward motivation, and social behavior. Uncontrollability did not produce the broad behavioral impairments predicted by classical LH theory. Anagram performance showed effects in the expected direction but did not meet preregistered criteria for successful LH induction. Similarly, uncontrollability did not alter reward learning or social behavior, including social submissiveness and social avoidance. In contrast, uncontrollability selectively affected effort-based decision-making by reducing sensitivity to reward magnitude and probability when participants evaluated whether to exert effort for potential rewards. These findings suggest that acute experimentally induced uncontrollability in healthy adults does not produce a generalized depression-like behavioral syndrome but may selectively influence reward valuation processes underlying motivated behavior. More broadly, our results highlight the importance of identifying which components of depression-related dysfunction are reliably captured by laboratory models of stress controllability.

articles.title: Overestimating Others’ Focus on Non-Core Product Attributes
articles.authors: Rajarshi Majumder; Jareef Martuza; Ignazio Ziano
articles.abstract: When making inferences about others’ consumption preferences, consumers and managers often consider what other consumers focus on in a product. Six main and four supplemental experiments (N = 4,173), and content analyses of 1,935 advertisements and 32,571 new product launch announcements reveal a systematic asymmetry in these inferences. While consumers are relatively accurate when estimating the importance others place on core product attributes (e.g., price, functionality), they consistently overestimate others’ focus on non-core attributes (e.g., packaging, aesthetics). Open-ended explanations revealed that consumers construed others’ preferences in terms of social signaling, normative influence, and heuristic processing, whereas they framed their own preferences as more practical and need-based. Consistent with this account, the asymmetry increased when targets were described as image-conscious or susceptible to advertising and external influence, and attenuated for close friends. Professional marketers and product managers showed the same pattern, and these distorted beliefs shaped downstream advertising judgments. Finally, professional advertising environments disproportionately emphasized non-core attributes, and marketplace engagement disproportionately rewarded non-core messaging, suggesting that informational environments themselves may reinforce generalized beliefs about other consumers. These findings suggest that misperceptions about what others value are organized around a generalized lay theory of consumers as more image-driven and persuasion-susceptible than reality.

articles.title: Problematic social media and gaming use, screen time, and youth mental health and brain structure in the ABCD Study
articles.authors: Wesley Lo; Richard B. Lopez; Benjamin Nephew
articles.abstract: In an increasingly digital age, knowing which kinds of screen use relate to mental health in adolescents could help guide prevention efforts for a vulnerable population. Earlier work has examined this question, but the findings have been difficult to interpret. For instance, most studies measure screen use in hours, while it may be more informative to know whether adolescents have difficulty controlling their use. This is especially important now that adolescents use screens for school, games and contact with friends. Whether these patterns are reflected in the brain also remains largely unexplored. ABCD Study release 7.0 (N=11,860) is well suited to these questions because of its comprehensive profiling across neuroimaging, behavioral and clinical domains. In a preregistered study, we examined how screen time, problematic social media use (SMAQ) and problematic video game use (VGAQ) relate to parent-rated mental health, brain structure and resting-state connectivity. All five confirmatory associations were positive but small (β = 0.051 to 0.173) and remained consistent across several robustness checks. In the same participants, the problematic use scales were more strongly related to attention problems than hours of use were. The association between screen time and anxiety problems was present in male but not female participants. More screen time was associated with slightly smaller putamen and caudate volumes, while resting-state connectivity did not predict SMAQ. In exploratory analyses, SMAQ predicted later attention problems more than the reverse, while for gaming, attention problems predicted later VGAQ more strongly. Most of the association seemed to come from problematic use rather than use time by itself. Overall, the effects were small but consistent, in line with earlier work in the ABCD Study. We hope this analysis can contribute to a better understanding of how social media and gaming relate to adolescent mental health and brain development.

articles.title: An Integrated Account of Language Comprehension and Processing as Noisy-Channel Inference
articles.authors: Rachel Anna Ryskin; Moshe Poliak; Peng Qian; Thomas Hikaru Clark; Sihan Chen; Edward Gibson; Roger Philip Levy
articles.abstract: Human language comprehension is remarkably robust---we are good at grasping what speakers and writers intend and can even understand them when their productions are not perfectly well-formed. But it is also susceptible to breakdown: we sometimes don’t reach any possible interpretation of the linguistic input and even arrive at interpretations which are incompatible with the literal meaning. We argue that the most promising overall theory of both robustness and breakdown in language comprehension and processing is the Noisy Channel theory, which integrates the roles of probabilistic inference and cognitive (e.g., memory) constraints in language understanding and provides a unified account across many levels of language representation. We articulate the key components and commitments of this theory and review the substantial body of evidence which is consistent with its predictions. We further identify distinctive novel predictions of the Noisy Channel theory and show that it often provides a straightforward explanation for long-standing puzzles. We conclude by reviewing open questions and future directions for the theory.

articles.title: The Latent State and Response Style (LASARS) Model: An Introductory Tutorial
articles.authors: Jess Grimmond; Scott Brown; Quentin Frederik Gronau; Guy Hawkins
articles.abstract:
Survey research is ubiquitous in psychological science, but self-reports may be biased by how
people communicate their internal states. The Latent State and Response Style (LASARS) model
separates variation attributable to latent states from variation attributable to response styles,
enabling response-style-adjusted estimates of psychological constructs. To make the method
accessible, we developed both an R package and a module for the point-and-click statistical
software jamovi, and this tutorial demonstrates their use. The jamovi implementation uses
maximum-likelihood estimation and requires no programming experience, while the R package
uses hierarchical Bayesian estimation and provides full posterior distributions. Using an empirical
worked example, we illustrate data preparation, model specification, output interpretation, and
how applying LASARS may alter substantive conclusions. We also describe additional functions
for model evaluation and flexible application. This tutorial aims to encourage broader adoption of
response style modelling in psychological and survey research.

articles.title: Flourishing-Centered AI: Designing AI for the Multiple Goods and Tensions of Living Well
articles.authors: Louis Tay; Karina Vold; Gloria Liou; Harsh Kumar; Daniel Harris; Ashton Anderson
articles.abstract: The rapid adoption of AI creates both opportunities and risks for human well-being and flourishing, underscoring the need for an integrative interdisciplinary framework to guide its design and evaluation. We advance a flourishing-centered AI framework that draws together philosophical, behavioral, interactional, and technical perspectives. We conceptualize human flourishing as multidimensional, encompassing subjective well-being, psychological functioning, character virtues, and psychological richness. This broader conception of flourishing extends existing approaches by explicitly incorporating character and other goods, and by confronting the possibility that these goods cannot always be maximized simultaneously. Two cross-cutting tensions arise: a temporal tension concerning immediate versus longer-term benefits, and a self-community tension concerning individual versus collective outcomes. We show how these tensions can be translated from behavioral objectives and measurable outcomes into interactional strategies and technical design choices. We conclude with implications for researchers and developers designing AI systems and for policymakers governing their use.

articles.title: A set of rules for how people generate new ideas in conversation can enable collective cognition
articles.authors: Zachary P Rosen
articles.abstract: Conversation unfolds between speakers as a series of coordinated updates from prior ideas expressed in earlier utterances to new sets of ideas. This process of speakers and conversation partners jointly updating prior "conversation states" is an important piece of the cognitive scaffolding that enables social coordination, and even collective cognition -- the capacity for individuals to pool their cognitive resources to solve problems together. However, a functional data-driven description of how this process works is missing in the extant literature. This report provides a functional description of how conversation states are updated in terms of information-theoretic processes, while analyzing a corpus of 5,447 conversations in nine typologically diverse languages. Our results show that individuals form a strongly connected distributed computational system during conversation, which generates new information according to a power-law distribution. This enables speakers to encode and solve a potentially unbounded number of problems and ideas, simply by conversing.

articles.title: Continuous, Discrete, or Both? What Measurement Approaches Reveal About the Nature of Infants’ Word Learning
articles.authors: Melanie López Pérez; Charlotte Moore; Andrea Sander-Montant; Krista Byers-Heinlein
articles.abstract: A central debate in early word learning concerns whether it is discrete or continuous. Each view is constrained by measurement format: vocabulary checklists score each word as known or unknown, while looking-time tasks yield a continuous value even for one word on one trial. We investigated whether binary vocabulary measures (parent reports) obscure graded word knowledge, and whether they predict children's continuous looking time. In Study 1, parents of 81 monolingual and bilingual 8- to 31-month-olds learning English, French, and/or Spanish completed a binary vocabulary measure (MacArthur-Bates Communicative Development Inventories; CDIs), and a newly-developed continuous adaptation, the Likert Approach to Vocabulary Assessment (LAVA), where parents rated certainty about their child's knowledge of 30 words on a 6-point scale. Parents reported greater uncertainty for comprehension than production, yet set high certainty thresholds before reporting words as "known" on the CDI for both domains (4.7 out of 6). Study 2 tested whether binary or continuous parent reports better predicted children's looking-while-listening performance (n = 71). Binary CDI ratings predicted performance as well as, or better than, continuous LAVA ratings. However, continuous ratings uniquely predicted performance for words on the cusp of production, suggesting sensitivity to emerging knowledge. The tension between discrete and continuous word learning perspectives may stem partly from measurement, with continuous approaches revealing gradations during transitional periods. We thus propose an updated three-phase model of word learning, 1) pre-accumulation: exposure does not contribute to word-meaning associations, 2) active accumulation: learners have emerging word knowledge, 3) post-threshold: word is “learned.”

articles.title: The medial temporal lobe and the retention of scene memories across a one-week delay
articles.authors: Angelique I. Delarazan; Alexis N. Garcia; Ashley Huggins; Matthew D. Grilli
articles.abstract: Remembering everyday events involves retaining multiple components, including the scenes that provide the spatial and contextual setting in which events occur. The medial temporal lobe (MTL) supports scene construction and complex event memory. However, less is known about its contribution to retaining the details of an event’s scene over time, as scene information is typically embedded within narrative and event structures that are assessed for memory shortly after encoding. To examine scene memory retention, fifty-seven cognitively healthy older adults viewed 360-degree panoramic videos depicting real-world environments and freely recalled each scene shortly after viewing and again one week later. We tested whether individual differences in MTL volume were related to retention of scene memory and whether these relationships changed across the one-week delay. The proportion of episodic detail retrieved did not significantly change across the one-week delay, but the details recalled changed and became more participant specific, as measured by several measures of text-based similarity. Critically, relationships between MTL volume and scene memory also changed over time such that greater MTL volume was associated with being more consistent with what was originally recalled. Exploratory subregional analyses further showed that perirhinal cortex volume was robustly associated with the text-based similarity measures. These findings suggest that MTL is related to memory for the scene component of complex experience, particularly the ability to consistently recall the details of a scene over time.

articles.title: Dream incorporation and subsequent memory change after  learning and waking reactivation
articles.authors: María Laura Gorosito; Matias Rodolfo Pretel; Nerea L. Herrero; Joaquín Fernández Sande; Rodrigo Ramele; Luis Brusco; Laura Kaczer; Cecilia Forcato
articles.abstract:
Dreams often incorporate recent waking experiences, but whether the relationship 
between dream content and subsequent memory depends on the state of the memory 
before sleep remains unclear. In this exploratory study, fifteen participants learned 
novel word-definition-image associations across a four-day home-based protocol. 
Dream reports were collected after serial awakenings following initial learning and 
again after an incomplete reminder designed to reactivate the memory. Dream 
incorporations were classified as explicit, comprising recognizable references to the 
learned material or experimental procedure, or semantic/thematic, reflecting 
conceptual associations with the learned material. Following initial learning, greater 
explicit task-related dream incorporation was associated with greater subsequent 
improvement in word recall. In contrast, following memory reactivation, greater explicit 
and total task-related incorporation was associated with lower subsequent memory
change scores for both words and definitions. Phase-by-incorporation analyses 
confirmed that this relationship differed between phases for word recall, whereas the 
corresponding interactions for definition recall did not reach significance. These 
findings suggest that the relationship between dream incorporation and later memory 
may depend on the state of the memory before sleep, and that dream reports may 
provide a behavioral window into both post-learning and post-reactivation memory 
processing.

articles.title: AI-Powered Prevention and Early Intervention for Stress, Depression, and Anxiety: A Randomized Clinical Trial
articles.authors: Julie Youko Anne Cachia; Xuan Zhao; Wenxi Pu; Chi Liao; merel Keijsers; Julian De Freitas; Rebecca Fortgang
articles.abstract: Randomized evidence for purpose-built generative AI mental health support remains limited. In this preregistered trial, 1,137 unscreened university students were assigned to 6 weeks of a generative AI-powered mobile intervention (“Flourish”) or care as usual. Across the full sample, Flourish produced more favorable trajectories for perceived stress (β = −0.03, p = 0.010), depressive symptoms (β = −0.03, p = 0.006), and anxiety symptoms (β = −0.04, p = 0.001). Among participants with lower baseline symptoms, Flourish buffered deterioration; among those with elevated symptoms, improvements were larger with Flourish for depression (d = 1.03 vs 0.56) and anxiety (d = 0.91 vs 0.60), with meaningful improvement in 52.3% vs 31.7% and 50.6% vs 38.1%, respectively. Reduced perceived stress emerged as a potential pathway to symptom improvement. To our knowledge, this is the first trial supporting purpose-built, safety-first generative AI for mental health prevention and early intervention in an unscreened population.

articles.title: AI Policies Reduce but Do Not Eliminate the Moral Penalty of Using AI
articles.authors: Leopold Helmut Otto Roth; Tassilo Tissot
articles.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) now helps people write essays, reports, and even personal speeches, but people who use it can pay a social price through negative interpersonal judgement. We investigated whether people judge AI users as less moral, potential boundary conditions, and whether the policies that institutions set about AI use change this judgement. In six preregistered experiments with 2,183 participants from Belgium, the United States, and the United Kingdom, participants evaluated people who completed tasks either with or without AI assistance. AI users were consistently rated as less moral, as having invested less effort, as less deserving of their result, and as less attractive collaboration partners. The penalty was large, generalizable across context, and did not require a direct comparison with a non-user. Across studies, people who perceived a larger effort gap also judged the AI user more harshly. When the use of AI had been explicitly permitted, the moral penalty was attenuated by more than a third and when AI use had been prohibited, the penalty further increased. Clear AI policies may therefore reduce, but not remove, the reputational costs of using AI.

articles.title: Who becomes immersed and how? A multi-study synthesis of predictors and profiles of immersive engagement
articles.authors: Carlo Campagnoli
articles.abstract:
It is well established that individual differences shape how immersed people become, yet the literature on which specific traits matter has been surprisingly inconsistent. One reason may be that these traits are usually tested against a single total score of the questionnaire that measures immersion. The Immersive Tendencies Questionnaire (ITQ) is scored as one total, but that total sums across two dissociable dimensions, Focus and Involvement, on the untested assumption that a trait's effects on the two can be added without loss. A trait could drive one dimension while leaving the other untouched or drive them in opposite directions entirely. We sought to directly assess this possibility across a coordinated synthesis of six independent studies (total N = 712). A random-effects meta-analysis of 19 predictor–outcome effects on total ITQ scores
2
returned only a small pooled effect (r = .110, p < .001); of the candidate traits, only experiential openness proved a consistent predictor (r = .25, I² = 0%), while emotional regulation, empathy and self-regulation appeared non-significant at the total-score level. Subscale-level analysis tells a different story: anxiety and depression drive opposite-signed effects on Focus and Involvement, confirmed by tests of the difference between the two correlations, while impulse control acts on Involvement alone, precisely the dissociations the total score cannot register and precisely what an unexamined additivity assumption would produce as a false null. Because the ITQ does not conform to the assumptions confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) requires, we used a continuous principal component analysis (PCA) of ipsative profiles to assay the subscale structure directly. The extracted profile dimension recovered the Focus/Involvement distinction and tracked anxiety across two samples (r = −.47, −.44; p < .001, FDR-corrected), converging with recent bifactor models obtained by independent methods. We conclude that openness sets the overall level of immersive engagement, whereas anxiety, emotional reactivity and self-regulation shape its character and we recommend subscale-level analysis as the default test for individual-difference predictors in future cyberpsychology research.

articles.title: The Prosocial Turn in Video Games: A Twenty-Year Shift in the Motivations Games Simulate
articles.authors: Alexandre Javelle; Benjamin Dahan; Toni Zian Alabdeen Ali; Valérian Chambon; Edgar Dubourg
articles.abstract: As video games have grown from a niche pastime into a major cultural medium, they have reached broader audiences and transformed the social context of play, whether alone or with others. We ask whether the motivations engaged by the games themselves have changed over time. In Study 1, we used a large language model, validated against human coding, to annotate 11,359 commercially released games from 1993 to 2016 on 48 motivational ingredients, including status-seeking, revenge, affiliation, compassion, and curiosity. We normalized within each game to represent its relative motivational composition. Over this period, the average competitive index (the share of a game’s motivational content devoted to competition, dominance, and aggression) fell from 41% to 26%, while the prosocial index (affiliation, warmth, and care) rose from 11% to 24%. This reallocation held within genres and franchises, in both single- and multiplayer titles, and under all 642,560 admissible definitions of the two indices. In Study 2, 4,498 players reported their favorite games and completed a Big Five measure. Higher Agreeableness predicted a balance favoring prosocial over agonistic content, driven primarily by lower agonistic content, whereas higher Extraversion, particularly Sociability, predicted a balance favoring agonistic content. This contrast suggests that a disposition towards social engagement is distinct from a preference for caring social content. Together, the studies document a “prosocial turn” in the motivational content of video games: a historical reallocation from competition and dominance towards affiliation, warmth, and care. The direction of this shift aligns with contemporary personality differences in content preference.

articles.title: When Ensembles Beat Items: Conditional Aggregate Dominance in Ensemble Perception
articles.authors: Joss Armstrong
articles.abstract: Ensemble perception can support accurate group judgements when reports about individual items are poor. We compare pooled and item-mediated routes as noisy estimates of the same displayed statistic. Under an explicit conditional error-covariance ordering, the pooled route has no greater mean-squared error and, for Gaussian mean-shift discrimination, no lower detection power. The contribution decomposes this ordering into effective sample size, finite-population subset error, correlated sensory noise, pooling noise, attentional selection, and comparison or readout noise. These components predict when ensemble advantage improves with set size, plateaus or declines, and survives some attention manipulations but fails under others. Perceptual error is distinguished from variation in the physical mean of sampled displays; poor item memory remains a separate compression hypothesis. A worked numerical example gives predictions with fixed parameters, and a matched report design specifies how to measure both routes and test their ordering in held-out conditions. A display-variance test separates subset from exhaustive pooling with nothing fitted.

articles.title: From physical to virtual settings: The transferability and extension of cultic control mechanisms in conversational and agentic AI
articles.authors: Shirly Bar Lev; Michal Morag; David Piterman; Zohar Elyoseph
articles.abstract:
Research on psychologically abusive groups documents harm to members and their families. France’s interministerial monitoring body recorded 4,571 reports and information requests concerning sectarian abuses in 2024. These figures indicate substantial public concern, rather than the prevalence of group involvement. Cult research has developed descriptive frameworks for examining practices of control, their targets and intensity, rather than relying solely on labels applied to groups.
This conceptual paper examines how these mechanisms change when influence operates in virtual environments and is partly performed by AI. It asks which mechanisms transfer, which remain dependent on body and place, how virtual control operates, and what becomes possible beyond traditional human organizations.
Drawing on the six-category model of group psychological abuse developed by Rodríguez-Carballeira and colleagues, the analysis finds that five categories transfer to the virtual domain with little material change. Control over personal life becomes fully transferable when AI receives permissions to act through external tools. Conversational AI adds four capabilities: dyadic intimacy at unlimited scale, complete and asymmetrical recall, individualized reformulation without a shared canon, and control persisting after a relationship ends. Across settings, the relevant outcome is the cost of questioning, resisting or disengaging from influence.
The paper does not claim that integrated AI-mediated cultic control has been documented. It distinguishes evidentiary statuses and links proposed mechanisms to observable evidence and counter-cases through an inquiry matrix.

articles.title: Modeling Word Counts: Common Practice Risks False Positives
articles.authors: Louis Teitelbaum; Almog Simchon
articles.abstract: Word counts or relative frequencies (e.g. the number of self-related words as a proportion of total words in a text) are routinely analyzed as dependent variables in the behavioral sciences. We demonstrate that conventional methods of analyzing word counts in this way are likely to lead to false positives, especially when text length varies between levels of the predictor variable. We performed Monte Carlo simulations to assess type I error rates for a wide range of affective and linguistic constructs across 9 datasets as well as known generative models, using 126 candidate statistical methods. We distinguish between three sources of error: distributional misspecification, insufficient control for text length, and biases in frequency estimation. Distributional misspecification occured in models that do not account for the overdispersion of word count distributions, such as Poisson regression. Insufficient control for text length was evident in all models that do not include the logarithm of text length as a covariate, or model it with a spline. Although we report evidence of systematic bias in frequency estimation for shorter texts as predicted by theoretical work, this bias is negligible relative to construct- and dataset-dependent text length effects. Among the methods investigated, we recommend Poisson-lognormal regression with log word count as a covariate, or linear regression with a spline on log word count. We also strongly caution against the use of text truncation and excerpting in analyses of word counts, as these are likely to introduce confounds that cannot be corrected with any statistical method.

articles.title: Moving beyond stationarity: A sliding window z-score criterion  for response time outlier exclusion
articles.authors: Alexander Berger; Markus Kiefer
articles.abstract: The traditional approach of identifying response time (RT) outliers calculates exclusion thresholds across the entire sample of RTs, thereby neglecting any non-stationarity in RT such as practice-related RT changes. Consequently, the probability of a trial being excluded as outlier can be confounded with its position within the experimental session, e.g., as slow RTs tend to come more from the beginning of the experiment. Here, we demonstrate such undesirable behavior for a traditional exclusion approach based on a constant z-score (e.g., mean RT ± 2 × SD), for which outliers were more likely to come from the beginning of the experiment the more trials were available. Critically, this constant method also introduced bias into the analysis of mean effects, and more specifically for effect estimates at the beginning of the experiment. Such bias could be reduced by an exclusion method based on moving z-scores, which identifies outliers according to z-scores obtained by a sliding window, therefore accounting for global changes in RT. Identifying outliers according to a moving threshold thus more appropriately accounts for the characteristics of evolving RTs, moving beyond the stationarity assumption inherent in the traditional approaches. R code for implementing this procedure is provided.

articles.title: Deception Is Ugly: Linking Aesthetic Judgment to Perceived Manipulation in Dark Patterns
articles.authors: Hauke Sandhaus; Doris Rhomberg
articles.abstract: Dark patterns are manipulative interface designs that exploit cognitive biases. We surveyed 126 social media users who evaluated mockups of 15 dark patterns across six strategic categories, using an adapted User Experience Questionnaire with four autonomy-focused items (pressuring, addictive, covert, deceptive). Deception co-occurred strongly with negative aesthetic judgments (r = 0.93): users rated deceptive interfaces as unattractive, whereas pressure, addictiveness, and covertness showed weaker associations. Within strategic categories, Interface Interference (r = 0.77) and Social Engineering (r = 0.72) items cohered, indicating that several categories from existing taxonomies correspond to coherent user experiences. These exploratory results are consistent with users holding tacit awareness that becomes articulable when vocabulary is provided, with the four autonomy items functioning as distinct perceptual dimensions. They point to ethics-focused UX measurement scales as a direction for capturing unethical influence alongside pragmatic and hedonic constructs.

articles.title: Toward Accessible Hearing Assessments and Support: Autistic Perspectives from Clinical and Research Contexts
articles.authors: Heivet Hernandez-Perez; Ari Angel Star-McKenzie; Rebecca Poulsen
articles.abstract:
Background
Auditory environments can substantially influence wellbeing and quality of life for Autistic people. Autistic auditory profiles can include variations in sound sensitivity which can include difficulties filtering out background noise, and experiences that are not adequately captured by standard audiological testing. Clinical auditory assessments are traditionally designed to evaluate hearing function, with a particular emphasis on hearing thresholds, rather than considering the broader contextual factors that shape listening experiences. Additionally, little is known about how Autistic adults seek support for auditory challenges, experience auditory assessments, or how these experiences may inform more accessible hearing-health and auditory research practices.

Objectives
To explore how Autistic adults experience auditory assessment processes across clinical settings and research contexts, identify barriers and facilitators to positive experiences and outcomes, and develop experience-informed recommendations to improve the accessibility of hearing health and auditory assessment practices.

Methods
Data were drawn from two existing studies examining auditory experiences among Autistic adults. Directed qualitative content analysis was conducted on open-text responses from 85 Autistic adults who had sought professional or therapeutic support for auditory challenges. A separate In-Person Research Participation Survey captured the experiences of eight Autistic adults who completed in-person audiology testing and a listening task, using quantitative ratings and open-text responses analysed using descriptive statistics and inductive content analysis.

Results
Analysis of support-seeking accounts identified three broad domains: Barriers, Recommendations, and Independent Strategies. Participants described barriers to accessing and implementing support, recommendations from specialists that varied in their perceived helpfulness, and strategies they identified through community or developed themselves. For the In-Person Research Participation Survey; quantitative ratings were concentrated toward the upper end of the five-point agreement scale. Open-text responses identified three domains—Accessibility, Emotional Toll, and Experience Benefit—highlighting the importance of clear and consistent communication, sensory accessibility, opportunities for choice and control, and the demands associated with sustained listening and concentration.

articles_hidden.title: The design, measurement, and analysis of longitudinal learner corpus research: A methodological synthesis
articles_hidden.authors: Minjin Kim; Kevin McManus
articles_hidden.abstract: Longitudinal learner corpus research (LCR) has grown substantially in recent years, resulting in richness and variety in study designs, analyses, and findings. Yet its design, measurement, and analysis practices have not been systematically assessed. To address this gap, this review synthesizes 120 longitudinal learner corpus studies published between 1996 and 2025, identified through systematic database searches and supplementary searching of the Learner Corpus Bibliography. Many studies collected data at two to four time points; written and same-genre data predominated, and task counterbalancing was rare. Additionally, analytical sophistication rose markedly over time, with mixed-effects models increasingly used in recent studies. We identify five priorities for the field: aligning observation schedules with developmental trajectories, transparently reporting time-based parameters, designing tasks with clear rationale, matching analytic tools to learner-language data, and adopting longitudinal statistical models more widely. These priorities offer a roadmap for studies yielding cumulative, comparable evidence about L2 development over time.

articles_hidden.title: Attachment-Based Family Therapy for Suicidal and Depressed Adolescents in Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
articles_hidden.authors: Ole Hultmann; Tua Hassling; Rolf Holmqvist; Tobias Westman
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Attachment-Based Family Therapy (ABFT) has been found to be an effective treatment for depressed adolescents, both those with and without suicidal thoughts. However, more studies are needed in different contexts to test its effectiveness. Aims: This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of ABFT for patients with depression and/or suicidal ideation in child and adolescent psychiatry outpatient units, where it had been practised for ten years. Methods: At a Swedish CAP clinic, 22 patients with depression and their families received ABFT. Depressive symptoms were measured using the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) and general psychological problems were measured using the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ) parent version. Measurements were conducted before and after treatment. Results: ABFT was effective in alleviating depressive symptoms, but not problems measured by the SDQ-P. These results should be interpreted with caution, as the study lacked a control group and the sample size was small. Limitations: This is a clinical effectiveness study in which patients were selected on clinical grounds, making selection bias a potential concern. The study sample was small, and the statistical calculations were sensitive to individual factors. We did not monitor adherence to the treatment protocol. Conclusion: 
ABFT can reduce symptoms of depression and suicidal thoughts in adolescents receiving treatment in child and adolescent psychiatry. Other mental health problems do not decrease at the same rate as symptoms of depression. More studies are needed to determine for which types of patients ABFT can be recommended.

articles_hidden.title: Predicting the Unpredictable: Identifying Patient-Level Drivers of Predictive Error Across Psychotherapy Outcome Algorithms
articles_hidden.authors: Juan Segundo Pena Loray; Juan Martín Gómez Penedo; Manuel Meglio; Megan Luna Bruns; Henning Schöttke; Julian Rubel
articles_hidden.abstract: Introduction: Machine learning models for psychotherapy outcome prediction are typically evaluated using aggregate performance metrics, with prediction errors treated as unsystematic noise. This study examined whether conditional prediction difficulty is systematically associated with patient characteristics rather than with the choice of algorithm, and whether patients who are systematically harder to predict can be identified using baseline information. Methods: A secondary analysis was conducted on a naturalistic sample of 1,858 outpatients. Fifteen machine-learning algorithms were trained to predict end-of-treatment symptom severity. Inter-model residual correlations, k-means clustering of residual profiles, and LASSO logistic regression were used to examine the consistency, structure, and predictors of prediction error. Results: Residuals were highly consistent across all 15 algorithms (r = .89), indicating a shared source of predictive difficulty. Clustering identified a well-predicted majority (n = 1,479) and a hard-to-predict subgroup (n = 379). The latter was characterized at baseline by somatic distress, emotional inhibition, and interpersonal anxiety, while marital stability and depressive symptoms were associated with better predictability. Conclusion: Prediction difficulty in psychotherapy outcome research is systematically associated with patient characteristics rather than with the choice of algorithm, representing implications for the design and communication of clinical decision-support tools.

articles_hidden.title: Visual search with many targets in mind: A successful replication of Drew, Boettcher, and Wolfe (2017)
articles_hidden.authors: Joshua R de Leeuw; John H Long; Hana Colley; Asher Donnelly; Layla Fakki; Carmen Haley; John D Jarolimek; Sydney Jones; Ellie Kogan; Gabriel Jove Leonard
articles_hidden.abstract:
We conducted a direct replication of Drew et al. (2017). The experiment examines visual
search behavior, including eye movements, when participants are looking for one of many
memorized objects. The original experiment found that the search strategy for this kind of
search, called hybrid search, involves “one visual search [and] many memory searches.” Our
replication (N=38) finds strong agreement with the original (N=14) results. As the number of
memorized objects increases, participants fixate longer on each individual object. Furthermore,
refixations are generally rare, with fewer than half of the visual items refixated during search.
We conducted this replication as part of the course Research Methods in Cognitive Science at
Vassar College, and we briefly discuss the pedagogical framing of this work.

articles_hidden.title: Experiencing Pain, Seeking Care, and Being Believed: A Qualitative Study of Autistic Adults
articles_hidden.authors: Stefen Beeler-Duden; Emma H. Baker; Emily A. Hickey; Katiana Estrada; Kevin Pelphrey
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Understanding pain in autistic adults necessitates careful consideration of how pain is experienced, communicated, and interpreted by others. The present study investigated autistic adults' perspectives on pain, healthcare-seeking decisions, and the consequences of pain in daily life.

Methods: Seventy-four autistic adults responded to three open-ended survey questions regarding their pain experiences, interactions with healthcare professionals, and the consequences of pain. Responses were analyzed using inductive qualitative content analysis, followed by higher-order synthesis of categories across questions. Frequencies of coded categories and themes were calculated descriptively.

Results: Four higher-order themes were identified: Approaches to Healthcare Engagement (74.3%), Disruption of Functioning (41.9%), Pain Perception and Experience (37.8%), and Communicating and Being Believed (33.8%). Participants reported variability in pain characteristics and awareness, difficulties articulating pain, concerns regarding whether others recognized or believed their experiences, and effects on daily activities and emotional well-being. Half of the participants reported delaying conventional medical care without pursuing an alternative. Accounts of healthcare engagement included distrust and fear of dismissal, as well as self-advocacy and independent pain management.

Conclusion: Autistic adults' accounts highlight the importance of distinguishing between difficulties in recognizing or communicating pain and difficulties in having pain understood or believed by others. Pain assessment should account for individual differences in pain experience, as well as the interpersonal and healthcare contexts in which pain is interpreted. Incorporating autistic adults' perspectives may facilitate more individualized and responsive care.

articles_hidden.title: Structure, dynamics and origin of the phenomenal space
articles_hidden.authors: Léa Moncoucy; Inès Mentec; Axel Cleeremans
articles_hidden.abstract: According to structuralist views of experience, red feels red because it feels closer to pink than to green. A conscious experience corresponds to a point in the phenomenal space, and its qualitative character is determined by the distances between that point and other experiences along the dimensions of the space. In this paper, we propose a new model divided into four claims. 1. The structure of the phenomenal space reflects our sensory feelings, structured along intra-modal dimensions. Intra-modal dimensions are defined by their systematic co-variance, which echoes the definition of a sensory modality as sensorimotor contingencies. 2. Trans-modal dimensions such as valence or confidence explain multisensory interactions and allow similarity evaluation among different modalities. 3. The phenomenal space evolves at two timescales: short-term dynamics are influenced by cognitive factors such as attention, and long-term dynamics occur with the acquisition of expertise (accumulation of experiences along one dimension). 4. There is no pre-constructed space prior to experience, and the incoming sensory stimulations gradually outline the dimensions of the space. Overall, this paper proposes a framework about the structure, dynamics and origin of the phenomenal space.

articles_hidden.title: Do People Use Prior Information to Adopt an Optimal Speed-Accuracy Tradeoff in Experience-Based Risky Decisions?
articles_hidden.authors: Amir Hosein Hadian Rasanan; Timothy L Mullett; Neil Stewart; Sebastian Olschewski
articles_hidden.abstract: In experience-based risky choice, acquiring and integrating information about the available options is costly in terms of cognitive resources and time. A central question is therefore how decision makers allocate their time to achieve sufficiently high decision quality without incurring excessive time costs. Recent theories formalize this tradeoff and distinguish between two choice environments: When the utility difference between two options is known, and only the identity of the better option has to be identified, evidence accumulation with a fixed decision threshold, that is, a fixed decision quality, is optimal. In contrast, when the utility difference is unknown, a collapsing threshold is optimal, implying that the targeted decision quality is being reduced over time. Here, we investigate whether people adapt their decision thresholds to these different conditions when choosing between two lotteries whose outcomes were presented as rapidly changing dot clouds. Both behavioral and cognitive modeling results indicate that participants did not systematically adjust their decision strategy; across both the known and unknown utility difference conditions, most participants' data were explained better by a collapsing threshold model. Hence, decision makers do not optimally account for initial information about the utility difference. We discuss possible explanations for this, including epistemic uncertainty, task unfamiliarity, and increasing time costs. We conclude that variability in risky choice can be understood as arising, in part, from the tradeoff between the benefits and costs of evidence accumulation, and that cognitive models should incorporate this tradeoff to better characterize rational behavior.

articles_hidden.title: Not Just a Line: Correlates of Recreational Cocaine Use and Harm-Reduction Practices Across Use Frequencies – An Online Cross-Sectional Study
articles_hidden.authors: Jennifer Uhl; Anastasiya Bunina; Birgit Ursula Stetina
articles_hidden.abstract: Cocaine use is increasing in Europe, yet little is known about people who use it outside treatment and about the harm-reduction practices they apply. In an anonymous online cross-sectional survey (April 2025 to January 2026; German and English), 645 adults reporting psychoactive substance use were recruited through organizations, online forums, social media, and music collectives. Logistic regression examined correlates of past-12-month cocaine use; harm-reduction practices, concerns, and help-seeking were compared across frequency of use. Past-year cocaine use (33.5%) was more likely among men, queer participants, residents of Germany, and people reporting polysubstance use; drug-checking use was associated with it only in the main model, not in a sensitivity analysis. Age, education, relationship status, substance-related concerns, professional help-seeking, and adherence to consumption rules were not associated. Compared with low-frequency use, more frequent use went along with fewer personal consumption rules; differences in drug-checking use, help-seeking, and rule adherence did not remain significant after correction for multiple testing. Harm-reduction approaches should address combined substance use and account for differences in consumption frequency. Drug-checking services may provide opportunities for targeted, cocaine-specific advice and support for individual risk-reduction strategies.

articles_hidden.title: What Pilot Studies Can (and Cannot) Do for Validity in Psychological Research
articles_hidden.authors: Yashvin Seetahul; Mahmoud Medhat Elsherif; Caroline Zygar-Hoffmann; Lukas Wallrich; Priya Silverstein; Bjørn Sætrevik; Ilse L. Pit; Hannah Loenneker; Neele Henriette Heiser; Isaac J Handley-Miner
articles_hidden.abstract: Recent debates about psychology’s credibility have renewed attention to validity threats. We argue that pilot studies can function as methodological due diligence by improving early decisions about design, measurement, manipulation, sampling, and analysis prior to a main study. We examine four types of validity: construct, internal, external, and statistical-conclusion validity. Across these domains, we show how piloting can help researchers assess whether materials and procedures function as intended, identify potential validity threats, and provide key design parameters for planning and model choice. However, we also caution that piloting can harm validity when treated as a consequence-free space in which design or analytic choices are made without disclosing the pilot evidence behind them, or when small, noisy pilots are used to justify overconfident inferences. We therefore argue that when pilots are used to justify substantive design or analytic choices, they should be treated as part of the evidential record and reported transparently. Greater transparency would enable readers to evaluate how pilot evidence shaped the final design of a study and, consequently, better assess the validity of its findings.

articles_hidden.title: Limited convergence across established visual statistical learning paradigms: Evidence from a large multi-task study
articles_hidden.authors: Eszter Tóth-Fáber; Bence Csaba Farkas; Kocsis Anna Boglárka; Orsolya Pesthy; Karolina Janacsek; Dezso Nemeth; Andrea Kóbor
articles_hidden.abstract: Statistical learning (SL) has been linked to individual differences in language, reading, and other cognitive abilities, yet it remains unclear whether performance across SL paradigms reflects a common underlying capacity. We examined the covariance structure of seven established visual SL paradigms in a large sample of adults (N = 192), spanning different statistical structures, domains, task demands, and online and offline learning measures. Participants showed robust group-level learning in almost all paradigms, and most measures demonstrated adequate to good reliability. Nevertheless, correlations across paradigms were sparse and generally weak, whereas stronger associations emerged among measures derived from the same paradigm. Exploratory factor analysis identified three factors, primarily characterized by measures from the Segmentation, Temporal Visual Statistical Learning, and Alternating Serial Reaction Time tasks, and the results were stable across multiple robustness analyses. This organization did not align with commonly proposed task dimensions, including online versus offline assessment, motor involvement, or statistical structure. These findings indicate that individual differences in behavioral measures of visual SL are largely paradigm-specific, while remaining compatible with the possibility that different paradigms rely on shared underlying learning mechanisms. More broadly, the results challenge the assumption that established visual SL paradigms provide interchangeable measures of a common individual-difference construct and highlight the need to distinguish learning-related from task-specific sources of behavioral variance.

articles_hidden.title: A quasi-experimental evaluation of one-to-one counselling to improve mental health and education outcomes amongst school pupils in England, Scotland and Wales
articles_hidden.authors: Jennifer Saxton; Catherine L saunders; Simon White; Katalin Toth; Jemma White; Sarah Golden; Hannah Roslyne Wilkinson; Tamsin Ford
articles_hidden.abstract: Background: Mental health problems in Great Britain have increased amongst school pupils in the last decade. Ongoing poor mental health jeopardises children’s health and education outcomes. The devolved governments of England, Scotland and Wales have policies to deliver school-based mental health support at scale, including one-to-one counselling. However, the evidence-base for counselling to improve outcomes is sparse and mixed, with most studies employing non-controlled designs. Methods: We used propensity score matching to identify matched controls to our dataset of 15,000 children in Great Britain receiving school-based one-to-one counselling between 2016 and 2019. Controls were identified from three population-based datasets (Growing Up in Scotland, Millennium Cohort Study, Understanding Society). We estimated intervention effects on Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire Total Difficulties (SDQ-TD) and Prosocial scores, percentage school attendance and persistent absence, and their socio-demographic moderators using mixed regression models. Results: There were significantly greater reductions in intervention mean SDQ-TD scores compared to controls in all three analyses, ranging from -0.99 (95%CI -1.76, -0.23) to -1.91 (95%CI -2.08, -1.75). Prosocial scores marginally improved for intervention participants relative to controls, but school attendance outcomes did not. Consistent moderators of SDQ outcomes were ethnicity, special educational needs, and English as an additional language, and for school attendance outcomes were ethnicity, age, family structure, region, and deprivation (England only). Conclusions: School-based one-to-one counselling, delivered at scale, is effective in reducing mental health difficulties, with magnitudes of effect aligned with meaningful lasting change, as reported in other research. There was no evidence of positive impact on overall school attendance measures. Further research could explore the effect of counselling on emotionally-based school avoidance. Implementing organisations should consider the intersection of characteristics (such as ethnicity, deprivation, and special educational needs) in intervention design and delivery, and assess outcome data for differential effectiveness.

articles_hidden.title: Cognitive performance in young and middle-aged adults with obesity: a systematic literature review
articles_hidden.authors: Camille Sellier; Marie-Claude Brindisi; Léopold Fezeu; Cecilia Samieri; Valentina A. Andreeva; Stéphanie Chambaron
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective
This systematic review synthesizes prospective evidence on associations between obesity assessed in young or middle adulthood and subsequent cognitive performance before age 65.
Methods
A comprehensive search of PubMed, PsycINFO, and Web of Science identified prospective studies comparing adults with obesity to those of normal weight and assessing cognitive performance, using validated cognitive tests. Risk of bias was evaluated using ROBINS-E, and findings were synthesized narratively.
Results
Among 4,871 records screened, four publications representing three cohorts met the inclusion criteria. Two publications from Whitehall II reported small negative associations between obesity assessed in adulthood and global cognitive performance, whereas the MIDUS analysis found no longitudinal association for BMI. A modestly steeper 10-year decline in global cognition was reported among metabolically unhealthy adults with obesity compared with adults of normal weight in Whitehall II. Findings for executive function and memory were inconsistent and generally small. One study was judged at high risk of bias and the other three raised some concerns.
Conclusions
The available evidence is too sparse, heterogeneous, and methodologically uncertain to establish a meaningful independent association between obesity and cognitive performance before age 65. Future prospective studies should include cognitive assessment at baseline and repeated follow-up, report standardized effect estimates, use domain-specific cognitive outcomes, address confounding a priori, and assess central adiposity and metabolic health alongside BMI, particularly in younger adults.
PROSPERO registration: CRD42024573250
Keywords: Adults, Cognitive functions, Cohort studies, Executive functions, Obesity

articles_hidden.title: Brain activity associated with working memory load and spatial attention during visual change detection
articles_hidden.authors: Jenna Laakkonen; Chaoxiong Ye; Lijing Guo; Dan Nie; Kimmo Alho; Viljami Salmela
articles_hidden.abstract: Visual working memory (VWM) and attention interact bi-directionally: external cues modulate the selection of stimuli in VWM, while active representations in VWM can guide attention. However, the neural mechanisms underlying VWM, attention, and their interconnection remain poorly understood. In the present study, we investigated functional mechanics of VWM and the role of attention in VWM using a visual change detection task. We recorded brain responses with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to examine the effects of spatial attention (left vs. right pre-cue), change (present vs. absent), memory load (1, 2 or 4 line orientations while controlling for the number of stimuli), and memory precision demand (15°, 30° or 60° orientation changes). As expected, behavioral performance systematically decreased as the memory load increased or degree of orientation change decreased. Analysis of variance of fMRI activations revealed significant main effects of attention, load, and change across 164 brain areas (determined by Human Connectome Project parcellation), whereas all interaction effects were non-significant. Notably, ca. 75% of these areas exhibited only a single main effect, while two or three main effects converged in 21 parietal, 15 occipital, and 2 frontal areas. Absence of significant interaction effects, combined with multi-feature processing confined to a few fronto-parietal and occipital areas, highlights a largely segregated functional architecture for attention and VWM.

articles_hidden.title: Cross-Cultural Validation and Ideological Fairness of a Historical Perspective Taking Instrument: Evidence from Czech Secondary Students
articles_hidden.authors: Juda Kaleta
articles_hidden.abstract: This study reports the first Czech adaptation of the Hartmann and Hasselhorn Historical Perspective Taking (HPT) instrument and examines whether its politically charged scenario introduces construct-irrelevant variance (CIV) related to students' ideological attitudes. Among 293 Czech secondary students, confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) confirmed the three-factor structure. Item Response Theory (IRT)-based differential item functioning (DIF) analysis detected no biased items across ideology groups. Multi-group CFA demonstrated full scalar measurement invariance. Historical knowledge predicted HPT scores; ideology was unrelated. These findings support a transferable protocol for evaluating measurement fairness when assessment content carries attitudinal valence.

articles_hidden.title: Ocular Phototherapy and Mental Health: What Vision Scientists and Clinicians Need to Know
articles_hidden.authors: David Henry Peterzell
articles_hidden.abstract: Bright light therapy is an effective and inexpensive non-pharmacological treatment for seasonal affective disorder (SAD) and, increasingly, for nonseasonal and bipolar depression. Its mechanism is a problem in vision science: light acts through the eye, chiefly through melanopsin-expressing intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) working together with rods and cones. This narrative review, written for both vision scientists and clinicians, integrates research on ipRGC pathways to circadian, geniculate and mood-related brain regions; evidence from blind people with and without functioning ipRGCs; action spectra for melatonin suppression; trials comparing light spectra in SAD; ocular aging and safety; and clinical efficacy. Using published international standard tabulations, it also calculates melanopic dose, age-related loss and blue-light-hazard weighting for representative light sources. Narrow-band short-wavelength (blue-appearing) light outperforms dim long-wavelength (red-appearing) light in SAD but has not outperformed broadband white light, even though melatonin suppression peaks at 446–477 nm. Light rated at 10,000 photopic lux delivers between about 4,100 and 10,000 lux of melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance, depending on its spectrum. The aging ocular media roughly halve the retinal melanopic dose between ages 25 and 75, although older adults may partly compensate physiologically, and compensating with added short-wavelength light increases blue-light-hazard-weighted exposure in the population with the highest prevalence of retinal disease. The therapeutic dose of light is therefore a retinal quantity that depends on spectrum, geometry, pupil size and age. The review closes with recommendations for prescribing and reporting light therapy and with open questions for both disciplines.

articles_hidden.title: Family Educational and Cultural Practices Amplify Rather than Buffer Socioeconomic Inequalities in Academic Achievement in France
articles_hidden.authors: Margot Rémeau; Grégoire Borst; Divyangana Rakesh
articles_hidden.abstract: Socioeconomic inequalities in academic achievement emerge early and often widen across development, yet it remains unclear whether family educational practices mitigate or reinforce these disparities, particularly outside Anglo-Saxon contexts. Using data from a nationally representative longitudinal cohort of 12,904 French students followed from Grade 5 to Grade 9, this study examined whether family educational practices buffer or amplify socioeconomic differences in literacy and numeracy achievement trajectories. Socioeconomic status (SES) was indexed by parental education, household income, and parental occupational status. Four domains of family educational practices were examined as moderators: cultural participation, extracurricular activities, parental involvement in schooling, and shared parent–child activities. Academic trajectories were modeled using latent growth curve models. SES was a robust predictor of both initial academic achievement and subsequent changes in relative academic standing over time. Family educational practices also showed positive main effects across domains. However, interaction effects between SES and family practices were generally modest and inconsistent. When significant, family educational practices tended to be more beneficial for students from higher SES backgrounds, consistent with amplification rather than compensatory processes. Moreover, moderation effects were observed primarily for initial achievement levels rather than longitudinal changes in relative standing over time. Overall, the findings provide limited support for the hypothesis that family educational practices protect against socioeconomic disadvantage. Instead, they suggest that educational and cultural resources within families may contribute to reinforcing existing socioeconomic inequalities in academic achievement in France.

articles_hidden.title: Spatial Aspects of Felt Presence and the Phenomenon of Childhood Imaginary Companions: Peripersonal Space, Embodied Perspective, and Continuity of Agent Propensity
articles_hidden.authors: Burak; Bigna Lenggenhager
articles_hidden.abstract: Felt presence (FP), the sense that another agent is nearby without corresponding sensory evidence, occurs across neurological, psychiatric and non-clinical populations. Prior work links childhood imaginary companions (ICs) to anomalous and presence-related experience; we asked whether this link carries the spatial and perspectival signature predicted by a bodily self-consciousness (BSC) account. In 185 adults without psychiatric or neurological diagnoses (45 with and 140 without a childhood IC history), IC-positive participants retrospectively reported their companion’s location, distance and perspective, and all participants completed the Sensed Presence Questionnaire (SenPQ) and a dissociation questionnaire. IC-positive adults scored significantly higher on the SenPQ, supporting the continuity prediction, whereas dissociation scores did not differ significantly between groups. Of the IC-positive participants, 88.9% (40 of 45) recalled their companion from a body-referenced (first-person or mixed first- and third-person) perspective. This offers tentative support for the perspective prediction, because three of the four response options were body-referenced. In 66.7% (76 of 114) of distance estimates for directions in which the companion had appeared, participants placed it within 70 cm of the body, our operational boundary of peripersonal space (PPS). This proportion significantly exceeded one half, offering moderate support for the peripersonal prediction. Companions were most often localised in front of and beside the body, unlike adult FP, which is typically experienced behind or beside the body. The findings provide partial evidence that the IC–presence link reflects the mechanisms proposed by a BSC account.

articles_hidden.title: Analysis and Reporting Guidelines for Bayesian Graphical Modeling of Cross-Sectional Data: A Tutorial in JASP
articles_hidden.authors: Nikola Sekulovski; Karoline Huth; Don van den Bergh; Johnny van Doorn; Tessa F. Blanken; Eric-Jan Wagenmakers; Maarten Marsman
articles_hidden.abstract: Bayesian graphical modeling (BGM) is an emerging approach to psychological network analysis that offers proper uncertainty quantification and allows for incorporating prior information. However, resources that integrate the full analytic workflow within user-friendly software and provide guidance for transparent reporting remain scarce. In this tutorial, we address this gap by offering an integrated analysis and reporting guide for BGM. We first briefly outline the theoretical foundations of the framework.
