We then introduce the updated Bayesian network analysis module in the open-source software JASP and demonstrate three core analyses using an empirical dataset: edge selection and parameter estimation, clustering analysis, and comparing networks across groups. For each analysis, we provide minimal template paragraphs for the Methods and Results sections. We conclude with recommendations for prior robustness analyses and open research practices.

articles_hidden.title: Genuine association or spurious responses? An experimental investigation of the association between cryptocurrency trading and Problem Gambling Severity Index scores
articles_hidden.authors: Maira ANDRADE; Leonardo Weiss-Cohen; Richard J. E. James; Leon Y. Xiao; Philip Newall
articles_hidden.abstract: Background and aims: Cryptocurrency trading has become a popular activity worldwide, despite being largely unregulated and posing high risks. Previous studies have correlated cryptocurrency trading with harmful gambling as measured by the Problem Gambling Severity Index (PGSI), but no experimental research has explored whether these represent genuine associations or are spuriously inflated by methodological weaknesses. Methods: In a large-scale pre-registered 2x2 online experiment (N = 4,781), we hypothesised that if observed correlations were driven by spurious responding, then they would be significantly weakened by screening out non-gamblers (compared to the unscreened control), and by explicitly instructing participants to not consider cryptocurrency trading as a form of gambling (compared to a no-instruction control). Cryptocurrency trading engagement was assessed via self-reported trading frequency, price monitoring frequency, and the number of coins owned over the past 12 months. Results: Results While screening significantly lowered reported PGSI scores, the association between trading frequency and the PGSI remained robust and statistically significant across all conditions, and was not moderated by screening or providing explicit instructions. Exploratory analyses found the same patterns with price monitoring frequency and the number of coins owned, and in a combined model with all predictors, trading frequency explained the most variance in the PGSI outcomes. Conclusions: Together, these findings provide strong support for a genuine association between cryptocurrency trading and harmful gambling. Financial and gambling regulators should consider this evidence when designing consumer protection frameworks for cryptocurrencies.

articles_hidden.title: The predictive value of trans related stressors and resilience factors for mental health outcomes – a machine learning approach
articles_hidden.authors: Felix Strakeljahn; Claudia Calvano; Alexandra Brecht; Björn Schlier
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Trans people experience elevated levels of mental health problems compared to the general population. Trans-specific psychosocial stressors and resilience factors have been shown to account for part of the variance in mental health. However, most studies have included only a limited subset of relevant stressors and resilience factors, leaving unclear both the amount of variance that can be explained by a comprehensive predictor set and which individual stressors and resilience factors are most informative for mental health outcomes.
Methods: A total of 447 adult trans individuals participated in a cross-sectional online study and completed measures assessing trans-specific stressors and resilience factors, as well as well-being, social functioning, and overall mental health problems. Prediction models were estimated using random forests within a nested cross-validation framework. Shapley additive explanations were applied to identify the most influential predictors for each mental health outcome.
Results: Prediction models based on psychosocial stressors and resilience factors, and demographic data achieved R² = 26% for well-being, R² = 32% for social functioning, and R² = 35% for overall mental health problems. Gender dysphoria, rumination about others’ perception, and internalized transnegativity consistently ranked among the five most important predictors across all models.
Discussion: Trans-specific stressors and resilience factors explain a substantial proportion of variance in mental health outcomes. Nevertheless, incorporating additional predictors, including general risk and protective factors for mental health, may further enhance predictive accuracy and thereby improve mental health prediction in this population.

articles_hidden.title: Towards precision psychotherapy: Leveraging session-level data to predict session-by-session treatment outcomes
articles_hidden.authors: Felix Strakeljahn; Tania Marie Lincoln; Niklas Jacobs; Celine Brandt; Kevin Hilbert; Katrin Bahlinger; Inga Frantz; Björn Schlier
articles_hidden.abstract:
Theoretical Background: Clinical support tools can potentially enhance cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) by providing session-by-session treatment recommendations. To enable such tools, prediction models are needed that can accurately track therapy outcomes based on assessable session data. This study developed models that predict session-by-session mental health levels and identified variables that influence these predictions.
Methods: We analyzed data from a monocentric, naturalistic therapy-process study of outpatients with affective, anxiety, and psychotic disorders (n=325) participating in up to 24 weekly sessions of CBT in routine care in Germany. Within a nested cross-validation approach, we used mixed-effect random forest models to predict session-by-session scores on a brief self-report measure of mental health (i.e., symptoms, mood, distress, functioning) assessed in the next session. Included predictors were baseline psychopathology, type of CBT interventions conducted in the prior session, and patient- and therapist-reported mechanisms of change (e.g., cognitive change, self-understanding, coping) assessed in the prior session. Variable importance was examined using SHAP values.
Results: The mixed-effects random forest predicting next-session outcome achieved an R²=0.25 across the test folds. The most influential predictors were baseline psychopathology and prior session self-reported behavioral mechanisms of change, i.e., engagement in meaningful/positive activities and coping.
Conclusion: Session-by-session prediction of mental health outcomes using routine outcome monitoring data yielded promising predictive accuracy. Self-reported mechanisms of change are particularly valuable for predicting session-by-session mental health levels. These findings may suggest that activating behavioral mechanisms of change in therapy may have a stronger impact on short-term mental health than activating cognitive mechanisms of change.

articles_hidden.title: Prevalence and Characteristics of Migraine in Postmenopausal Women:  A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Abbie Louisa Greenwood; Ruth Jensen; Megan Crawford; George Gorrie; Victor Kenji Medeiros Shiramizu
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background
Migraine can improve after menopause, but prior reviews assessing postmenopausal migraine were limited by the available literature, finding improvement in some populations and worsening in others following menopause. This review and meta-analysis investigated the effect of 1) Menopausal status (premenopausal, postmenopausal) on migraine prevalence 2) Menopause Hormone Therapy (MHT) use in postmenopause on migraine prevalence 3) Menopausal status (premenopausal, postmenopausal) on migraine characteristics (headache frequency, migraine frequency, pain intensity).

Methods
Searches were conducted across Medline, Scopus, Web of Science and APA PsychINFO in accordance with PRISMA guidance. Included studies measured the prevalence or characteristics of migraine in postmenopausal and/or premenopausal women. Random effects meta-analysis of proportions was conducted to analyse migraine prevalence data, and Robust Bayesian Meta-analysis for migraine characteristics data. Study quality was assessed by modified version of JBI critical appraisal tool for prevalence studies. 

Results
From 1174 records screened, 30 studies were included (16 prevalence meta-analysis, 10 characteristic meta-analysis). The pooled prevalence of migraine was 22% for premenopausal and 16% for postmenopausal women, but the prevalence was not significantly different between the groups. Migraine prevalence was significantly higher in postmenopausal women using MHT compared to those not. Robust Bayesian meta-analysis showed strong evidence for an effect of menopausal status on migraine characteristics (BF10 = 63.84, g = -0.31), with postmenopausal women exhibiting more severe migraine than premenopausal women, weak evidence in favour of heterogeneity (BFrf= 1.54), and weak evidence against publication bias (BFpb = 0.72). There was weak evidence in favour of a moderation effect of measurement of migraine characteristic used (BF = 1.35) and weak evidence against a moderation effect of study quality (BF = 0.45).

Conclusion
Migraine prevalence did not differ significantly but was consistently reported as more severe in postmenopausal relative to premenopausal women. Whether this results from different (clinical, non-clinical) samples used in studies or reflects an overall increase in severity in migraine populations in postmenopause is unknown and requires longitudinal investigation. Future studies should consider comorbidities, menopausal symptoms, time since menopause, surgical menopause populations as well as MHT type and initiation to understand migraine course across postmenopause.

articles_hidden.title: Unique and common qualifiers in the lexical differentiation of blue and brown in American English: Corpus evidence at the vision–language interface
articles_hidden.authors: David Henry Peterzell; Anke Marit Albers; Sean Isamu Johnson; Galina Paramei
articles_hidden.abstract: Most languages categorize a nearly continuous color spectrum using a small set of basic color terms (BCTs). Several languages (e.g., Russian, Greek, Italian) lexicalize two or more basic BLUE categories, distinguishing light from dark blue, a split English is usually said to lack. No such split has been found, yet speakers may differentiate blue shades in usage by attaching “light” and “dark” to blue more than to other terms. Using the Corpus of Contemporary American English (COCA), we extracted the 11 English BCTs with their most frequent preceding collocates (pre-2020 release, ~560 million words, five genres) and quantified qualification by all qualifiers, correcting for non-chromatic uses of color words and qualifiers alike. Although light blue and dark blue do not denote separate basic categories, blue is the most heavily qualified BCT overall and attracts a far wider variety of unique chromatic specifiers (navy, cobalt, cerulean) than any other, mirroring how finely English speakers divide the BLUE region in naming. Green and brown are heavily qualified too, and brown most heavily of all, but through common, largely achromatic modifiers rather than unique specifiers, a pattern we link to its being a constitutively dark, lightness-defined color with lightness-based subcategories. The contrast replicates on the current, larger COCA release (~993 million words, eight genres) with an independently constructed qualifier classification, and survives a dominance criterion applied to full-depth collocate lists. We argue that color-term basicness is gradient rather than discrete, and that corpus structure offers a naturalistic window onto the vision–language interface.

articles_hidden.title: The Role of Community Pharmacists in Identifying and Managing Insomnia and Facilitating Access to Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I) – a Systematic Review
articles_hidden.authors: Adebunmi Ogunnowo; Sukvinder Kaur Bhamra; Gurprit Lall; Aiste Steponenaite
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: 
Insomnia affects approximately 10% of the global adult population, leading to progressive health complications. As community pharmacists' roles evolve, their role in managing insomnia remains limited.

Objectives:
To review and evaluate the evidence on the role of community pharmacists in the management of chronic insomnia, including their role in facilitating cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I).

Methods:
A review of databases including PubMed, Scopus, MEDLINE, PsycINFO and Web of Science was conducted from inception to August 2025. Studies examining community pharmacists’ involvement in chronic insomnia management which met the inclusion criteria were narratively reviewed.

Key findings:
Of 129 articles screened, nine met the inclusion criteria. Three main themes emerged: community pharmacists could identify insomnia through patient counselling, deprescribe inappropriate hypnotics and sedatives, and, in some settings, deliver or signpost patients to CBT-I. One study reported a significant reduction in Insomnia Severity Index scores from 18.2 to 7.9 (p < 0.001), following pharmacist-led cognitive behavioural therapy. However, implementation was limited by a lack of standardised protocols, defined referral pathways and time constraints. 

Conclusions:
Community pharmacists can contribute to chronic insomnia management and improve access to evidence-based care, but this has not been widely adopted. This review highlights a gap between pharmacists’ capability and ability to implement such services. Recommendations include standardised approaches for insomnia screening, defined referral pathways and sustainable funding models. Addressing these barriers could enable community pharmacists to improve insomnia management.

Keywords: CBT-I | sleep | insomnia | community pharmacist | cognitive behavioural therapy | pharmacy practice

articles_hidden.title: Questionable mediated effect of dispositional optimism on psychological resilience: A comment on Wang et al. (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen
articles_hidden.abstract: Drawing on the covariance matrix reported by Wang et al., I reassessed the empirical basis of their mediation model linking dispositional optimism to psychological resilience. I demonstrate that the observed covariance structure can be reproduced by a theoretically different latent-variable model that does not rely on the directional mechanism proposed in the original article. In this alternative account, self-reported dispositional optimism, self-efficacy, adaptive coping, and psychological resilience are conceptualized as indicators of a broader construct, core self-evaluation. The results illustrate a broader inferential problem in psychological research: multiple theoretically plausible models may provide equally adequate explanations of the same correlational pattern. Consequently, observational associations alone offer limited grounds for preferring one explanation over competing alternatives. Researchers should therefore routinely evaluate alternative models when drawing inferences about psychological mechanisms from nonexperimental data.

articles_hidden.title: Color Vision for Human Factors Engineering: When Color Helps, When It Hurts, and for Whom
articles_hidden.authors: David Henry Peterzell
articles_hidden.abstract: Color vision serves everyday tasks, from judging food and reading skin to segmenting scenes and reading signs, displays, and data. Designers use color in safety codes, interfaces, visualizations, lighting, and interiors, but practice often outruns evidence. I review when color helps, when it hurts, and for whom. Color helps when it carries information that luminance and form do not, as in judging ripeness, guiding search, and supporting scene memory. It hurts at isoluminance, in fine detail, in clutter or conflict, in non-uniform colormaps, and when it is the only carrier of critical information. Engineers have exploited these limits, as in chroma subsampling, and ignored them at a cost, as in color-only safety codes. Who benefits varies widely: color vision deficiency is common, anomalous trichromacy spans a continuum of severity, discrimination declines with age, and appearance and naming vary among color-normal observers. Component color codes, intelligence-test materials, and aviation color-vision standards illustrate these lessons. I contrast robust effects of illumination on alertness with weak or failed claims about surface color, mood, and performance, propose design principles for human factors engineering, and grade the evidence behind common claims.

articles_hidden.title: Divided attention during encoding constrains the benefits of interim testing for subsequent learning
articles_hidden.authors: Bernhard Pastötter; Karl-Heinz Bäuml
articles_hidden.abstract: Retrieval practice can enhance learning of subsequently studied target information, a phenomenon known as the forward testing effect or test-potentiated new learning. The present study examined whether this effect depends on attentional engagement during encoding. In two experiments, participants studied three lists of unrelated words (Experiment 1) or three educationally relevant prose passages (Experiment 2). After the first two learning blocks, they either restudied the material or were tested on it. Attention during encoding of the final target material was manipulated by a concurrent secondary task. Under full attention, interim testing enhanced recall of the final target material in both experiments and improved performance on a final knowledge transfer test in Experiment 2. Under divided attention, these effects were reduced in Experiment 1 and eliminated in Experiment 2. The findings indicate that the beneficial effect of interim testing depends critically on attention during encoding of the latter studied information.

articles_hidden.title: Classroom Group Meditation and Frontal EEG Power-Envelope Networks: A Large Scale Hyperscanning Study
articles_hidden.authors: GAO JUNLING; Yilin Zhang; Hank Leung; Kin Cheung Lee; Chun Chi Poon; Bonnie Wai Yan Wu; Hin Hung Sik
articles_hidden.abstract: Portable electroencephalography (EEG) allows neural activity to be recorded from whole classrooms, but correlated activity across students can arise from shared instructions, parallel changes in arousal or common artefact rather than interpersonal coupling, and dyads within one class are not independent observations. In this exploratory analysis, single-channel frontal EEG was recorded during eyes-closed rest and guided group meditation in twelve classroom sessions at four schools (194 students; 9–23 per session). For each session and band (alpha, theta, delta, beta), sparse partial-correlation networks among participants were estimated from 140 consecutive 2-s band-power values with the Graphical Lasso, using one condition-blind penalty for both conditions. The primary outcome, positive network strength, was compared between conditions with the session as the unit of inference, using exact sign-flip tests and false-discovery-rate control across bands. No band differed between meditation and rest (alpha: mean session difference = 0.00006, 95% CI [−0.00083, 0.00096], raw p = .887, q = .939). No band differed after calibration against circular-shift surrogates or when one penalty was applied to all sessions, and alpha stayed null when any one session was removed. Along the penalty path, 9 of the 12 sessions changed the sign of their own alpha difference. A tuning-free mean pairwise correlation, calibrated against circular-shift surrogates, also showed no condition difference in any band. These data do not show that brief group meditation changes interparticipant EEG organisation in classrooms, and they indicate that per-session penalised network summaries need penalty-path and tuning-free checks before they are interpreted.

articles_hidden.title: Two separable axes of intervention in a dependency-ordered recovery geometry
articles_hidden.authors: Hiroki Saito
articles_hidden.abstract: A treatment can start a recovery or carry one further, and outcomes alone do not say whether these are actions on the same quantity. We ask this of a model motivated by catatonia, in which twenty-five inpatients recovered through five capacities in one fixed order and whose two effective treatments have no known dynamical representation. The model is an evidence-coupled bistable cascade on a dependency chain: each capacity is bistable, the threshold falls as evidence consolidates, and recovery propagates from a root by diffusive coupling. Two quantities are taken as intervention coordinates, an excursion applied to the root and the coupling between adjacent capacities, with the evidence coordinate closed to input by assumption; we show that they act on disjoint regions of state space. While every capacity is below threshold, a maximum principle forbids any non-negative diffusive coupling, on any graph and in either direction, from crossing the switching surface, so an acute conversion requires an excursion. With the root restored and the downstream chain collapsed, propagation is governed by one exact criterion, the prevailing threshold squared over four, because the first-stage equilibrium condition factorises; the weakest coupling sets where recovery stops, the same discriminant gives the first-stage eigenvalue and the inverse-square-root passage time through the fold, and the coupling is identifiable from the resting first stage. Eight falsifiable predictions are separated into consequences of the theorems, predictions needing an added clinical correspondence, and predictions needing a latent quantity measured; exploratory comparisons with published data bear on two of them.

articles_hidden.title: Affective Inertia Varies with Momentary Social Context: Evidence From Two Experience-Sampling Studies
articles_hidden.authors: ZhaoXuan Shang; Pedro Pan; Francisco Da Silva; Lois Choi-Kain; Marcos S. Croci; Marcelo Brañas; Eurípedes C. Miguel; Haya Fatimah
articles_hidden.abstract: Affective inertia refers to the degree to which affect carries over from one moment to the next and is typically modeled as a fixed, person-specific parameter. However, emerging evidence suggests that it may vary across time and context. Social context is a likely source of such variation, as people often rely on others to regulate their emotions, but whether inertia varies with everyday social context has rarely been tested. We examined whether momentary social context moderates affective valence inertia in two experience-sampling studies. Study 1 included 315 adolescents and young adults from a Brazilian high-risk cohort (2020–2021), and Study 2 included 803 adults from Austria, Germany, and Italy (2020). Social context was measured as being with others at each prompt in Study 1 and as social interaction since the previous prompt in Study 2. In both studies, Bayesian multilevel autoregressive models showed that social context was associated with more positive momentary valence and weaker overall valence inertia. Piecewise models further estimate positive and negative valence inertia separately, showing that social context was associated with weaker negative valence inertia in both studies, whereas its moderation of positive valence inertia was not credible in either study. Although the difference between these two moderation effects was only credible in Study 2, both studies linked social context to a weaker negative affect inertia. Overall, our results suggest a context-sensitive view of affective inertia and suggest that treating inertia as a fixed parameter may overlook meaningful within-person variation.

articles_hidden.title: Leveraging ecological momentary assessment and dynamic structural equation modeling to identify idiographic antecedents of child irritability and defiance
articles_hidden.authors: Shannon Shaughnessy; Spencer C. Evans
articles_hidden.abstract:
Irritability and defiance are common youth mental health problems that are associated with negative outcomes throughout the lifespan. Idiographic assessments can identify unique predictors of psychopathology, particularly when combined with quantitative methods and real-time assessments. The present study applies single-case dynamic structural equation models (DSEM) to parent-report ecological momentary assessment (EMA) data, identifying person-specific predictors of irritability and defiance. 

Two case examples were selected for analyses: “Kevin,” a 6-year-old boy with attention problems, and “Molly,” a 7-year-old girl with elevated hyperactivity. Parents reported on their child’s emotions, behaviors, and activities 3×/day for 30 days, with >90% compliance. DSEM analyses tested how each child’s current activity type predicted their irritability and defiance, both concurrently and over time.

For Kevin, media use predicted higher concurrent irritability and was a trend-level predictor of defiance, whereas active play predicted lower concurrent irritability and was a trend-level predictor of defiance. In contrast, for Molly, eating was a significant predictor of lower concurrent irritability but higher subsequent irritability. Sleeping was also a predictor of lower subsequent irritability for Molly.

In this proof-of-concept analysis, results showed that Kevin and Molly each had unique proximal predictors underlying their irritability and defiance. These rich idiographic findings, which would be missed by traditional methods, suggest implications for personalized treatment (e.g., regulating screen time and encouraging outdoor play for Kevin; consistent eating and sleeping schedules for Molly). Combining real-time assessment with advanced quantitative methods could lead to more effective interventions for Kevin, Molly, and children and families broadly.

articles_hidden.title: Facilitating Meditation with Focused Ultrasound Neuromodulation: A Sham-Controlled Crossover Study in Long-Term and Novice Meditators
articles_hidden.authors: Joshua Cain; Micah Johnson; Amirvala Tavakoli; Tracy Brandmeyer; Ninette Simonian; Geena Wang; Jezabel May; Alexander Bystritsky; Shinzen Young; Joseph Lacoste Sanguinetti
articles_hidden.abstract: Sustained contemplative practice confers well-documented psychological and physiological benefits, yet the experiential deepening that motivates practitioners can require many hours of practice, and mastery is not assured. Methods that accelerate training would broaden access to these benefits and could also test mechanism: the posterior cingulate cortex (PCC), caudate, and anterior insula are implicated in meditation, but only correlationally. We used low-intensity transcranial focused ultrasound (FUS) to ask whether reversibly perturbing each region shifts meditative experience in real time. In a single-blind, sham-controlled, counterbalanced crossover design, long-term practitioners of insight meditation in the S.N. Goenka Vipassana tradition (LTMs; n = 36) and meditation-naïve novices (n = 12; an exploratory cohort; meditation experience not randomized) received 12 minutes of inhibition-biased (5% duty cycle) FUS to the PCC, bilateral caudate, or bilateral anterior insula, or sham, in separate sessions during hour-long meditation. Every ~4 minutes, participants rated meditative depth (anchored from “extremely shallow” to “extremely deep”) and intensity (relative to their normal experience, along any dimension), with autonomic, mood, and trait measures as secondary outcomes. Sham-relative changes in rating trajectories were tested with generalized linear mixed models and false discovery rate (FDR)-corrected contrasts. In LTMs, caudate stimulation produced a significantly steeper rise in depth than sham and insula stimulation; in novices, PCC stimulation produced a significantly steeper rise in depth than sham, caudate, and insula stimulation, such that the caudate-versus-PCC difference in depth slopes differed significantly between groups, reversing in sign. No target altered intensity relative to sham, insula stimulation had no sham-relative effect on meditation, and post-session mood and trait measures were unchanged. Autonomic effects were modest and did not account for the meditative effects, and expectation of benefit did not differ across conditions in LTMs. FUS neuromodulation can causally and region-specifically accelerate meditative deepening, with the effective target differing by meditation experience (caudate in LTMs, PCC in novices), a dependence that may reflect practice itself or its correlates. Tempered by the single-blind protocol, the small novice cohort, and effects extending beyond sonication, these findings establish proof-of-principle for neuromodulatory facilitation of meditation and motivate individualized, closed-loop applications.

articles_hidden.title: Evaluation of Shared Autonomy and Tactile Feedback on a VR Realistic Physics Simulation of Upper Limb Prosthesis
articles_hidden.authors: David Crevillén Hernández; Alex Pasquali; Davide Bargellini; Roberto Meattini; Cosimo Gentile; Camilla Arnaud; Laura Zapparoli; Ionela Bara; Fabio Egle; Claudio Castellini
articles_hidden.abstract: Despite their functional capabilities, myoelectric upper-limb prostheses still present high abandonment rates. Combining user-generated motor commands with algorithmic assistance for grasp control (shared autonomy), or providing tactile feedback about grasping force, may enhance users’ sense of agency over the prosthesis, a key component of prosthesis embodiment (integration of the prosthesis into the bodily self). Understanding these effects in intended users is therefore important for developing prosthetic assistance.  We investigated these effects in 58 age- and gender-matched participants: 29 without and 29 with unilateral transradial amputation. Participants performed an object-repositioning task using a physics-based virtual reality simulation of a myoelectric prosthesis under four conditions combining two motor control modes (direct user control or algorithm-assisted shared autonomy) with two vibrotactile feedback modalities (continuous or pulse-width-modulated vibration).  Sense of agency was assessed through self-report ratings and a perceived temporal compression task. Additional measures included placement accuracy, gaze behaviour, embodiment, and phantom-limb experience. Shared autonomy increased self-reported agency in controls but decreased it in participants with amputation. Tactile feedback modality showed no significant effect on sense of agency measures. Greater phantom-limb control and embodiment of the phantom limb were associated with higher self-reported agency. Placement accuracy was higher in participants with amputation and under direct control. Direct control outperformed shared autonomy with continuous vibration in controls and with pulse-width-modulated vibration in participants with amputation. In controls, pulse-width-modulated vibration also yielded higher accuracy than continuous vibration under shared autonomy. These population-specific responses may partly reflect previous myoelectric-control experience. Prosthesis development therefore requires consideration of functional performance and users’ perception of the device, alongside longitudinal clinical evaluation to determine how these responses change with continued use.

articles_hidden.title: Phantom limb behaviour and gaze during obstacle avoidance: obstacle shunning and tolerance after upper-limb amputation
articles_hidden.authors: David Crevillén Hernández; Manfredo Atzori; Steffi Weidt; Emily S. Cross; Gianluca Saetta
articles_hidden.abstract:
Phantom limb sensations persist in most amputees and offer a window into how the body is represented without sensory input from the missing limb. In this state, vision may help resolve conflicts between the perceived body and the physical world. In obstacle tolerance (OBT), the phantom remains present despite overlapping with physical matter; in obstacle shunning (OBS), it retracts or disappears. Whether these experiences extend beyond subjective perception to visual attention during action remains unclear.
We tested whether OBS and OBT are associated with distinct gaze and task-performance patterns during obstacle avoidance. Fifteen individuals with transradial amputation (7 OBS, 8 OBT) and 29 able-bodied controls physically executed or imagined a limb repositioning movement while avoiding an obstacle. We recorded gaze using mobile eye-tracking and quantified obstacle-directed dwell time using automated obstacle segmentation and fixation detection. We analysed trial duration and attention shifts between the obstacle and the limb or environment.
Bayesian mixed-effects models showed that participants with OBT spent less time looking at the obstacle when using the affected rather than the intact limb during motor execution. They were also more likely to make three or fewer attention shifts with the affected-limb, suggesting reduced obstacle monitoring when phantom–object overlap is tolerated. Participants with OBS took longer than controls during both motor execution and motor imagery.
These findings suggest that OBS and OBT are associated with distinct action-related visuospatial strategies. Phantom–object relations appear to extend beyond subjective experience to the visual and temporal organisation of behaviour around physical objects.

articles_hidden.title: Functional neuroimaging as a tool to understand social determinants of health in cognitive aging and ADRD: a scoping review
articles_hidden.authors: Jade E. Jenkins; Adea Rich; Isabella Manrique; Shirine Moukaled; Natalie L. Marchant; Owen Carmichael
articles_hidden.abstract: The social, structural, and physical conditions in which individuals live, work, and age, collectively termed social determinants of health (SDOH), are associated with risk of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD). Differences in brain function in later life may offer understanding of how SDOH become biologically embedded and confer differential ADRD risk. However, how functional neuroimaging techniques have been used to study SDOH in cognitive aging and ADRD has yet to be systematically characterized. We therefore conducted a scoping review. Three databases were searched, 2,930 articles were screened, and 41 studies were included. Education was the most frequently studied SDOH domain, accounting for 65.9% (k = 27) of studies, followed by economic and occupation (k = 9, 22.0%), social and community (k = 5, 12.2%), food (k = 4, 9.8%), and physical environment (k = 3, 7.3%). Of the 41 studies, five (12.2%) examined multidomain determinants and one study (2.4%) examined three determinants each from different domains. Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) was most frequently employed (k = 31, 75.6%), followed by electroencephalography (EEG; k = 7, 17.1%), and magnetoencephalography (MEG; k = 4, 9.8%). One study (2.4%) employed a multimodal approach, while none used functional near-infrared spectroscopy. Resting state paradigms (k = 27, 65.9%) outnumbered task-based (k = 14, 34.1%) and most studies were cross-sectional (k = 38, 92.7%). The predominant focus on education, fMRI, and cross-sectional designs highlights many opportunities for future investigation of how SDOH may be associated with later life brain function.

articles_hidden.title: Adapting familiar object use to altered structure under different viewing conditions
articles_hidden.authors: Riccardo; Irene Sciulli; Annalisa Bosco; Patrizia Fattori; Alessia Tessari
articles_hidden.abstract: Using a modified familiar object requires learned actions to be reconciled with its current structure. We examined this problem using six everyday objects and altered counterparts designed to preserve recognisable identity and function while changing the relation between graspable and functional parts. Forty-six participants grasped and demonstrated object use in one of three conditions: continuous vision, immediate action after visual occlusion, or action after a 3-s delay without vision. Reach-to-grasp kinematics, manual spatial exploration and use errors provided complementary measures of performance; kinematic analyses included 45 participants and four object pairs. Errors occurred almost exclusively with unusual objects, which also elicited more exploration. No statistically significant object-type effect was detected in the measured kinematics. Reduced visual availability was associated with more exploration and lower peak transport velocity, whereas the condition effect on maximum grip aperture depended on the statistical model. Exploratory successive-condition contrasts identified changes in exploration and grip aperture after removal of online vision; evidence for an additional retention cost was inconclusive. No selective amplification of the unusual-object cost by viewing condition was detected. Together, the measures identify behavioural consequences of altered structure–function relations while leaving their effects on pre-contact movement uncertain. The findings identify difficulties in adapting familiar actions to altered objects and motivate assessing demonstrated use and exploration alongside grasping when investigating object usability.

articles_hidden.title: Domain-general object encoding ability explains shared variance between perception and memory factors
articles_hidden.authors: Conor J. R. Smithson; Andrew Tomarken; Isabel Gauthier
articles_hidden.abstract:
Domain-general object recognition ability (o) is an individual’s capacity to tell apart similar
objects. O has been measured using tasks that make strong demands on either perception or
memory. Both types of tasks ought to require precise encoding of high-level visual details.
However, the assumption that each task type measures perception and memory to a differing
extent has not been tested, nor has the critical assumption that they both tap into the same
high-level visual ability when other relevant abilities are controlled. An online sample (n = 275)
completed a battery of perceptual and memory type object recognition tests alongside tests of
low-level perception, working memory, and general intelligence. Preregistered structural
equation models were used to examine the overlap among abilities. Perception and memory o
tests loaded onto two separable factors, with the perceptual o factor relating to low-level visual
perception and the memory o factor relating to working memory. Both o factors were strongly
correlated, and remained so when general intelligence, low-level perception and working
memory abilities were controlled. These results are consistent with the view that both types of
tasks measure the same o ability in addition to either perception or memory ability. General
intelligence explained a large share of the ability to make high-level visual discriminations, but a
substantial proportion of variance remained independent. The results may be taken to suggest
that both perception and memory o tests measure a domain-general, high-level encoding
ability.

articles_hidden.title: Changing Contributions of Emotion and Reward Information to Learning Through Adolescence
articles_hidden.authors: Camille Phaneuf-Hadd; Elizabeth A. Phelps; Leah Somerville
articles_hidden.abstract: From childhood to adulthood, individuals’ learning and decision-making may be differentially impacted by two salient value signals for adolescents: emotions and rewards. This study superimposed these information sources to assess their independent and joint influences on learning and choice processes. Participants ages 8 to 22 years completed a reinforcement learning task, in which monetary rewards conveyed information integral to making reward-maximizing choices, while emotional expressions conveyed information incidental to this goal. In some conditions, emotion and reward invoked congruent approach-avoid tendencies; following either information source promoted making reward-maximizing (“correct”) choices. In other conditions, emotion and reward invoked incongruent approach-avoid tendencies; following the emotion cue impeded reward capture. Participants completed several measures indexing the persistence of emotion and reward information on choice and evaluations of these signals. Statistical and computational models revealed that emotion-reward incongruence hampered early learning through an incidental emotion bias on value estimates. The emotion bias decayed as reward learning progressed in adolescents and adults but endured in children. Moreover, reward-based choice increased with age across the additional measures. Although participants of all ages were initially hindered by incidental emotion cues, adults’ shift toward prioritizing integral reward outcomes indicates that goal-relevant information comes to dominate choice with age.

articles_hidden.title: Effects of Handgrip Effort on Perceptual Judgments and Metacognitive Performance in Older Adults
articles_hidden.authors: Andrew Yi-an Sun; Mohammad Dastgheib; Xiaoping Hu; Ilana J. Bennett; Weiwei Zhang; Brian Maniscalco; Megan A. K. Peters; Aaron Seitz
articles_hidden.abstract: Here we examined how physical-effort induced arousal may have a differential impact on perception and metacognition in older adults. While arousal has been shown to enhance some aspects of perceptual performance in young adults, it can also disrupt metacognitive performance. However, both perceptual and metacognitive functions decline with age, alongside deterioration of neural systems that regulate arousal (e.g., Locus Coeruleus-Norepinephrine; LC-NE). Thus, it is unclear how physical-effort induced arousal influences perceptual performance and metacognitive efficiency in older adults. To test this, we had participants complete two perceptual discrimination tasks (auditory and visual), which involved judging whether two sequential stimuli were the same or different, and subsequently rating their confidence in their same/different response. At the start of each trial, arousal was manipulated by instructing participants to maintain either a low or high hand grip force on a dynamometer. We fit psychometric functions to characterize perceptual performance between grip levels and used the Relative Psychometric Function (RPF) analysis framework to characterize metacognitive ability while controlling for perceptual performance. Across tasks, high grip increased psychometric thresholds, but not psychometric slopes. On the other hand, metacognitive efficiency increased under high grip and was numerically larger in the auditory task, which appeared to be driven by increased error awareness during the easiest stimulus level. Together, these findings suggest that acute arousal can disrupt perceptual performance but enhance metacognitive efficiency in older adults.

articles_hidden.title: Testing Whether Reported Treatment Effects are Robust to Item-Level Heterogeneity
articles_hidden.authors: Peter Francis Halpin; Joshua B Gilbert
articles_hidden.abstract: This paper addresses the situation in which treatment effects are reported using educational or psychological outcome measures comprised of multiple questions or “items.” Drawing from item response theory, we distinguish among three estimands of potential interest: (a) a treatment effect on the latent variable representing the construct of interest, which is referred to as impact, (b) test-level treatment effects computed using aggregates of assessment items (e.g., the unweighted mean), and (c) item-level effects. We show that test-level treatment effects and impact are generally not equivalent estimands in the presence of item-level treatment effect heterogeneity. Consequently, failing to distinguish these estimands can have important implications for the validity of research studies. To address this issue, we propose a diagnostic test to infer whether test-level treatment effects are robust to item-level heterogeneity. We illustrate the use of the test with a case study. We also provide some initial evidence about the prevalence of this issue using a small meta-analysis. Results from the meta-analysis indicated that treatment effects based on the unweighted mean of assessment items often biased upwards when compared to a robust altnerative, and that this pattern was more apparent with researcher-developed assessments than independently developed assessments.

articles_hidden.title: Navigating Dynamic Risks: Outcome Monitoring and Evaluation under Escalating Risk
articles_hidden.authors: Corinna Lorenz; Nicola Kristina Ferdinand
articles_hidden.abstract:
Real-world risk-taking unfolds through sequences of decisions where stakes escalate incrementally. Yet most ERP research examines isolated outcomes, leaving neural processing of accumulating risk poorly understood. We developed an ERP-adapted Columbia Card Task enabling precise temporal analysis of feedback processing across consecutive outcomes, systematically manipulating gain amounts, loss amounts, and loss
probability while recording EEG in 25 participants. We measured early outcome detection via the feedbackrelated negativity (FRN) and reward positivity (RewP) and later evaluative processing via the P3b.

Early outcome processing depended on the potential loss amount. FRN amplitudes differentiated between
positive and negative outcomes when large losses were at stake but not when losses were small, an effect carried by more pronounced responses to negative outcomes under large losses. The RewP showed a similar but less well supported pattern. Gain amount and loss probability did not modulate early components, and we found no evidence that they changed across the feedback sequence. In contrast, the P3b was larger for negative than for positive outcomes, and this difference increased across the feedback sequence as risk accumulated, without evidence for a dependence on the stakes. Exploratory analyses did not provide consistent evidence that individual risk propensity modulated these patterns.

With early processing scaling with the consequences at stake and later evaluation increasingly focusing on negative outcomes as the feedback sequence progresses, these findings suggest that outcome monitoring under escalating risk is not a fixed response to outcome valence.

articles_hidden.title: Moving Beyond the “Candidate Event Crisis”: Estimating the Combined Effects of 25 Life Events on Personality Trajectories
articles_hidden.authors: Keely A Dugan; Anqing Zheng; Matt Saxsma; D. A. Briley; R. Chris Fraley
articles_hidden.abstract: Life events are theorized to play an important role in personality development (Roberts & Nickel, 2017). Over the past two decades, research on event-related personality change has largely relied on a “candidate event approach,” estimating the effects of a small number of major life events modeled in isolation. Yet, recent meta-analytic evidence suggests that individual life events—even those that are intuitively impactful—tend to have very small effects on trait change (e.g., getting married, retiring; Bühler et al., 2024). People’s lives, however, consist of far more than a handful of “big days”; instead, they comprise a rich collection of experiences that may collectively shape who people become. Drawing inspiration from molecular behavior genetics—which moved beyond candidate gene studies towards polygenic models—the present study used analogous methods to model the poly-experiential nature of personality change. Using data from 4,904 adults who completed monthly assessments of the Big Five traits and 25 life events over two years, we conducted a poly-experience index (PXI) analysis and an Experience-Wide Complex Trait Analysis (ECTA), estimating the combined influence of many life events on trait change. PXIs accounted for 1-2% of the variance in trait change for neuroticism and conscientiousness—modest in absolute terms, but between 8 and 16 times greater than the variance explained by any single, “candidate” event. ECTA accounted for 1-2% of the variance in change for all Big Five traits except agreeableness. Implications of these findings for future research on life events and personality development are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: The Association Between Cardiorespiratory Fitness and White Matter Integrity Across the Lifespan: A Systematic Review
articles_hidden.authors: Rafaela Marchini de Oliveira; Curt Lox
articles_hidden.abstract:
White matter deterioration is a hallmark of cognitive aging and a core feature of many
neurodegenerative disorders. Cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) has emerged as a modifiable factor
that may support white matter integrity across the adult lifespan. This systematic review, using a
narrative synthesis, examined findings from 24 studies, identified through a systematic search of
PubMed, Web of Science, and PsycINFO databases, examining the association between
objectively measured CRF and neuroimaging-based white matter structure. Results revealed a
consistent positive relationship between higher CRF and stronger microstructural integrity,
particularly in late-myelinating tracts such as the corpus callosum, cingulum, and longitudinal
fasciculi. These associations were minimal in young adulthood, mixed in midlife, and most
robust in adults over 60, suggesting an age-dependent neuroprotective effect that strengthens
across the lifespan. Higher CRF was also linked to reduced white matter hyperintensity (WMH)
burden in older populations. While cross-sectional evidence for this relationship was largely
consistent, findings from randomized controlled trials were considerably more mixed, with most
intervention studies failing to detect group-level improvements in white matter microstructure
despite confirmed fitness gains. These findings underscore the potential of CRF as a nonpharmacological strategy to preserve brain health and mitigate cognitive decline with age. Future
research should adopt longitudinal and multimodal designs to clarify causal mechanisms and
identify age-specific moderators of these effects.
Keywords: cardiorespiratory fitness, white matter, fractional anisotropy, aging, aerobic exercise

articles_hidden.title: Dynamic learning from good and bad outcomes peaks and persists in adolescence
articles_hidden.authors: Katie Oshins; Tejas Savalia; Michelle Sauceda; Grace J. Yin; Alexandra O. Cohen
articles_hidden.abstract: Learning good and bad associations and updating them amidst change facilitates adaptive behavior. Differences in sensitivity to salient, dynamic information from the environment may influence how learning unfolds. Cross-species research suggests that adolescents, relative to younger and older individuals, may exhibit more persistent learned negative and positive associations. However, direct within-person comparisons of valenced learning processes are scarce, and the mechanisms underlying developmental differences in the persistence of learned associations remain unclear. In adults, the persistence of negative associations has been linked to individual differences in how people use experience to infer the structure of their environment. Developmental changes in these same latent-structure inference processes may underpin greater persistence of valenced associations during adolescence. To test this, participants ages 10-25 years completed a Pavlovian learning task in which distinct cues predicted gain, loss, or neither, followed by extinction, during which outcomes ceased. Conditioned responses to both positive and negative associations peaked and took longer to extinguish in late adolescence, near age 19. Negative associations were similarly robustly learned in young adults and weakly persisted in a new extinction context in early adolescence. While a shared latent-structure inference process was observed across valences, age-related differences in the tendency to attribute changes in reinforcement contingencies to multiple latent states mirrored the persistence of valenced associations in adolescence. These findings suggest that while both positive and negative outcomes shape dynamic learning across age, valenced learned associations more strongly influence behavior and cognition during adolescence, as individuals learn to independently navigate a changing world.

articles_hidden.title: Bilingualism and Cognitive Ageing: Domain-Specific Benefits After Controlling for Education and Lifestyle
articles_hidden.authors: Xinyu Liu; Umit Aydin; Christos Pliatsikas
articles_hidden.abstract: Lifelong bilingualism has been proposed as a cognitively enriching experience that mitigates age-related declines in cognitive abilities; however, the evidence remains mixed due to issues such as small samples, absence of effects in younger samples, and not accounting for confounding factors (e.g. education). Here we address these issues by examining adults aged 18-88 from the Cam-CAN dataset in two ways: by comparing monolinguals to bilinguals (N=390) and by examining bilingual experience as a continuous factor with a newly devised metric (N=460). Generalised additive models assessed fluid reasoning, ecological multitasking, and verbal abstraction. Increased age was associated with declined fluid reasoning and multitasking, but better verbal abstraction. Compared to monolinguals, bilinguals showed better preserved fluid reasoning in older age, suggesting decelerated cognitive decline, and higher verbal abstraction scores.  Our results help refine theories on the effects of bilingualism on cognition by showcasing that are likely to emerge in older age only.

articles_hidden.title: Rightward Saccades Distort the Scaffold of Spatial Working Memory in ADHD
articles_hidden.authors: Simar Moussaoui; Adam Frost; Matthias Niemeier
articles_hidden.abstract: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is typically characterized by executive dysfunction, yet emerging evidence points to spatially asymmetrical features of cognition. We examined whether transsaccadic working memory (tWM), the mechanism that integrates visual and motor signals across eye movements, shows directional vulnerability in ADHD. Participants with ADHD completed a spatial tWM task in which memory arrays (one or three items) were presented before leftward, rightward, or fixation trials, and repositioned a probe to the remembered target location. For comparison, data from a previously tested neurotypical sample were included in group-level analyses. Errors were decomposed into systematic and unsystematic components. Compared to controls, ADHD participants showed a modest but reliable rightward-saccade disadvantage, with greater systematic distortions after rightward than leftward eye movements. Saccades disrupted working memory in both groups, but the typical load-dependent increase in unsystematic error observed in neurotypical participants was absent in ADHD. Two complementary interpretations may account for this asymmetry. The integration-imbalance hypothesis attributes it to weakened right-hemisphere contributions to spatial working memory, which impair integration of left-hemisphere oculomotor and right-hemisphere spatial signals during rightward saccades. Alternatively, the anchoring-disruption hypothesis suggests that rightward eye movements destabilize the spatial scaffold anchoring remembered locations, producing geometric distortions without increased error. Together, these findings identify a direction-specific fragility of visuomotor-cognitive coupling in ADHD not explained by general capacity limits. More broadly, they reveal a partial neglect-like pattern of transsaccadic vulnerability: selective impairment for rightward saccades without a left-field deficit—highlighting the utility of oculomotor paradigms for revealing hidden spatial asymmetries in neurocognitive function.

articles_hidden.title: Expected but not rewarded: Limited uptake of open science practices as hiring criterion in a national sample of academic job advertisements
articles_hidden.authors: Bianka Crnković; Bernt Damian Glaser; Anastasia Bredenbrock; Agata Bochynska; Max Korbmacher; Wietske van der Ent; Ingebjørg Anjadatter Iversen; Sebastian J. Eikeland; Carmen Simonsen; Heemin Kang
articles_hidden.abstract: Despite a growing emphasis on the importance of open science practices, their integration into academic hiring criteria remains unclear. To better clarify this, we analyzed 1356 job ads for academic positions from Norwegian higher education institutions in 2023 and 2025 for mentions of open science experience as desired or required qualifications. Across both years, less than 5% of job ads mentioned open science skills as desirable or required. Furthermore, there was no statistically significant change in the proportion of open science practice mentions in the positions advertised between 2023 and 2025. However, job ads for more senior positions were increasingly likely to mention open science as a favorable or required skill. These results indicate that the recognition for open science skills is mainly reflected in the hiring for senior academic positions in Norway, but to a limited extent, and with no indication that this has increased with the adoption of open science policies by the government, national funding bodies, and research ethics committees. Consequently, we recommend that institutions more closely align their stated commitments to open science by encouraging open science as an evaluation criterion for all levels of academic positions.

articles_hidden.title: Validation of the Turkish Version of the YFAS 2.0 and Item-Level Insights for Short-Form Development
articles_hidden.authors: Burak kemal Ateş; Meltem Anafarta-Şendağ
articles_hidden.abstract: This study presents the first comprehensive Turkish adaptation and psychometric evaluation of the Yale Food Addiction Scale 2.0 (YFAS 2.0). A total of 346 adults completed an online survey including the YFAS 2.0, measures of maladaptive eating, impulsivity, depressive and anxiety symptoms, and social desirability. Translation followed established cross-cultural adaptation procedures, and psychometric analyses examined factorial structure, internal consistency, test–retest reliability, and convergent and discriminant validity. Food addiction (FA) prevalence was 9.3%. Confirmatory factor analysis supported the original unidimensional structure of the 11 diagnostic criteria, with strong factor loadings (.73–.94) and good model fit. Internal consistency (KR-20 = .86) and test–retest reliability (ICC = .70) were adequate. FA symptoms were found correlated with related constructs, including BMI, depressive and anxiety symptoms, emotional and uncontrolled eating, and impulsivity— particularly urgency—demonstrating convergent validity. Weak but significant correlations emerged with cognitive restraint and (lack of) perseverance, whereas no meaningful associations were observed with sensation seeking or social desirability, providing evidence for discriminant validity. Item-level analysis of the short-form item set indicated largely comparable but partially shifted highest-loading items relative to the original mYFAS 2.0 configuration, suggesting possible cultural or linguistic influences on item functioning. Overall, findings indicate that the Turkish YFAS 2.0 is a valid and reliable measure for assessing addictive-like eating in non-clinical adult populations. The scale performs similarly to previously validated international versions and provides a robust instrument for future research on food addiction, emotion-related eating, and associated psychological correlates among Turkish-speaking individuals.

articles_hidden.title: The art of permeability: A computational distinction between depersonalisation and advanced meditation
articles_hidden.authors: Fedal Saini; Hagar Tal; Ruben Eero Laukkonen; Matthew Sacchet
articles_hidden.abstract: First-person reports reveal a surprising convergence between symptoms of depersonalisation disorder (DPD) and certain forms of advanced meditation (AM). In both, individuals describe a fading, and even disappearance, of the ordinarily stable sense of being an embodied self. Yet the experiential tone and functional consequences strikingly differ. In DPD this alteration is endured as distressing alienation, while in AM it is deliberately cultivated towards psychological transformation and flourishing. We propose that this difference stems from opposite configurations of interoceptive permeability along the same computational axis. In DPD, defensive attenuation of ascending interoceptive precision limits the influence of bodily evidence on higher-level inference and stabilises a detached self-model. In AM, sustained practice increases the influence of bodily evidence on higher-level inference, allowing interoceptive signals to reshape and at times loosen the processes that sustain the sense of self. We account for meditation-related depersonalisation, a documented adverse effect of contemplative practice, by emphasising that increasing interoceptive precision without the regulatory conditions that render it tolerable reproduces the configuration that anchors the DPD pole. Finally, we outline the insula-prefrontal axis as a plausible substrate for this regulation. Clinical neuroscience has not characterised the regime in which bodily evidence constrains the self-model without recruiting defensive withdrawal, and advanced meditation provides a foundation from which to address this gap.

articles_hidden.title: Language, Cognition, and Other Ways We Think:  Anendophasia and the Functions of Inner Speech
articles_hidden.authors: Johanne Sofie Krog Nedergaard
articles_hidden.abstract: Much of our current understanding of inner speech – including much of what is presented in Kompa’s Language, Cognition, and the Way We Think – hinges on it being both pervasive in and important for cognition, with the two often being linked. As the argument goes: if inner speech is ubiquitous, it must be important, and if inner speech is important, everybody must have it. However, the observation that some people experience little to no inner speech makes this foundational notion less solid. Individual differences in inner speech have in recent years come into focus both in the public sphere and in the inner speech research field. While viral posts and clips are generally framed in a sensationalist manner rather than in the spirit of scientific inquiry, the specific perspectives and questions that come up in such public discussions are highly relevant for researchers as well. Scientists and philosophers have studied differences in how people experience “thinking” for a long time (see e.g., Aveling, 1927; Bartlett, 1927; Pear, 1927; Roth, 1965), and a subsection of the inner speech research field is already occupied with describing how the characteristics of inner speech within individuals vary by task demands (Fernyhough, 2004; Hatzigeorgiadis et al., 2011; Theodorakis et al., 2000; Yao, 2025). However, trait-level differences in the experience and use of inner speech have received less attention. The finding that some people experience little or even no inner speech deserves attention since, if true, it has serious consequences for theories about the (facilitative and even necessary) role of inner speech in human cognition generally. In this commentary, I will first outline the current evidence for the existence of people with anendophasia, as we have coined the phenomenon in question, and then contextualise anendophasia with regard to some of the functions of inner speech presented in Kompa’s Language, Cognition, and the Way We Think. I will argue that the existence of anendophasia is a serious challenge for theories claiming that consciously experienced inner speech is necessary for metacognition, self-reflection, self-knowledge, and reflexive, higher order, conscious thinking. I will then discuss four possible ways of dealing with this challenge.

articles_hidden.title: Linking Error Estimation for Mean-Geometric Mean and Pairwise Haberman Linking Across Multiple Time Points in the 2PL Model
articles_hidden.authors: Oskar Engels; Oliver Lüdtke; Alexander Robitzsch
articles_hidden.abstract: Longitudinal assessments link test forms through common items. Under item parameter drift, linked ability means and standard deviations depend on the item selection, adding a linking error (LE) to the standard error (SE). Treating mean-geometric mean linking and pairwise Haberman linking across three time points in the two-parameter logistic model as M-estimators, this article derives closed-form LEs and sandwich estimators of LE, SE, and total error (TE). Sandwich and item jackknife LE estimators are bias-corrected for person sampling, including dependent samples. In a simulation study, SE-based intervals undercovered increasingly with sample size, bias-corrected jackknife TE intervals reached acceptable coverage almost everywhere, and sandwich-based intervals undercovered with few items. Longitudinal mathematics data illustrate the estimators, with the LE exceeding the SE.

articles_hidden.title: Time Perspective as a Transdiagnostic Process Across Mental Illnesses and Associated Personality Traits: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Yi Yang; Siu Ching Wong; Hongen Ma; Irene Vassiliou; Ingrid Obsuth; Aja Louise Murray
articles_hidden.abstract: Time perspective refers to a cognitive and emotional orientation toward the past, present, or future, shaping how individuals interpret experiences, set goals, make decisions, and regulate behavior. Given its proposed links to diverse mental illnesses and related transdiagnostic personality traits, this systematic review and multilevel random-effects meta-analysis examined the transdiagnostic role of time perspective. In total, 191 publications (1,718 effect sizes) between January 1990 and March 2025 were included. Lower Future-Positive time perspective showed broad and consistent associations with higher internalizing symptoms, addiction, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms, externalizing symptoms, and impulsivity (rpooled = −.063 to −.314). In contrast, higher Future-Negative time perspective was primarily associated with higher internalizing symptoms (rpooled = .520). Higher Present-Hedonistic time perspective showed more condition-specific associations and was correlated with addiction, PTSD symptoms, and impulsivity (rpooled = .147 to .350). Higher Present-Fatalistic (rpooled = .158 to .299) and higher Past-Negative (rpooled = .170 to .431) time perspectives demonstrated the broadest transdiagnostic associations spanning internalizing symptoms, addiction, PTSD symptoms, externalizing symptoms, and neuroticism. Lower Past-Positive time perspective was specifically associated with higher internalizing symptoms, externalizing symptoms, and neuroticism (rpooled = −.168 to −.201). Effect size differences across mental illnesses and related personality traits indicated distinct time perspective profiles across conditions. Overall, Present-Fatalistic, Past-Negative, and Future-Positive time perspective emerged as highly transdiagnostic, whereas Present-Hedonistic and Past-Positive time perspective showed more condition-specific associations. These findings support the transdiagnostic relevance of time perspective and highlight the value of incorporating it into theoretical models and potentially into clinical practice.

articles_hidden.title: Cross-species social learning and its implications for the study of animal traditions
articles_hidden.authors: Mathieu Charbonneau; Dominique Guillo
articles_hidden.abstract: Social learning is a widespread capacity in the animal kingdom and has been extensively studied in the last decades, with evidence amassing that several non-human animal species can develop traditions and even cultures of their own. While definitions of social learning typically do not demand that it occurs exclusively between conspecific individuals, to this day most research has focused on interactions between same-species individuals. In contrast, the capacity to learn from individuals of another species, or heterospecific social learning, has received less attention, but this trend has started to shift. Here we review the growing research literature concerning social learning between non-human animals using a rigorous definition. We make the case that the study of heterospecific social learning promises to open new avenues of research and provide novel insights beyond those offered by the study of conspecific social learning. To do so, we organize our discussion around Tinbergen’s four questions, i.e., those of mechanisms, survival value, phylogeny, and ontogeny. Finally, we conclude by defining and examining the intriguing but counter-intuitive idea that heterospecific social learning can lead to the development and maintenance of behavioural traditions spanning across species, opening the door for the possibility of interspecific cultural evolution.

articles_hidden.title: Between the Spectrum and Mental Health: A Narrative Review of the Relationship between Autism Spectrum Disorder and Neuropsychiatric Comorbidities
articles_hidden.authors: Beatriz Cruz de Paula; Gabriel dos Santos Félix; Bruna Rabelo Ribeiro Domingues; José Aparecido da Silva; Priscila de Medeiros; Renato Leonardo de Freitas
articles_hidden.abstract: Individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) present a high prevalence of neuropsychiatric comorbidities, particularly anxiety disorders, depression, and Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). These conditions substantially intensify the clinical, functional, and psychosocial challenges associated with the autism spectrum across the lifespan. This study aimed to analyze, through a narrative review of the literature, the association between ASD and these comorbidities, as well as their impacts on mental health, daily functioning, and overall quality of life. The literature search was conducted in the PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science databases, prioritizing recent and methodologically relevant studies addressing this topic. The findings indicate that symptomatic overlap between core ASD features and co-occurring psychiatric disorders complicates early identification, differential diagnosis, and clinical management. This overlap often leads to delayed treatment and suboptimal outcomes, underscoring the need for integrated, developmentally sensitive, and personalized diagnostic and therapeutic approaches. In addition, the literature highlights significant structural barriers, including a shortage of trained specialists, limited access to multidisciplinary services, and the lack of targeted public policies, all of which hinder the provision of adequate care for this population. In conclusion, multidisciplinary interventions, combined with social inclusion strategies, community-based support, family and caregiver guidance, and the promotion of neurodiversity, are essential to improve emotional well-being, functional autonomy, and quality of life for individuals with ASD. Such efforts also have a positive impact on families and caregivers, contributing to more equitable and effective mental health care.

articles_hidden.title: From working memory to long-term memory: The role of focused attention and intentionality
articles_hidden.authors: Caro Hautekiet; Klaus Oberauer; Christian Nicolas Leon Olivers
articles_hidden.abstract: Although working memory (WM) and long-term memory (LTM) closely interact, the mechanisms by which WM representations are transferred into durable LTM traces remain unclear. It has been hypothesized that directing focused attention to information in WM strengthens its LTM traces. However, evidence suggests that focused attention offers at best a small benefit for LTM. Here, we propose that attention is necessary but insufficient. Specifically, we hypothesize that when people want to remember information for later, focused attention in WM will benefit LTM more, as it might enable strategic maintenance processes such as elaboration. In three experiments, the first phase consisted of a WM task in which participants memorized four real-world images on each trial. Focused attention was manipulated via retro-cues, and we controlled for testing effects by omitting the WM test on half of the trials. In a second phase, following a brief disruption task, LTM was assessed. Intentionality was manipulated by leaving one group unaware of the LTM test while another group was informed about it before the WM phase (Experiments 1 and 2) or were informed and could earn a financial bonus based on LTM performance (Experiment 3). While attention substantially improved WM performance, it offered only a small benefit for LTM performance; this effect did not interact with intentionality. Thus, these findings confirm that focused attention by itself hardly contributes to creating durable LTM traces, and show that intentionality is most likely not the missing factor.

articles_hidden.title: The Neural Correlates of Implicit Emotion Regulation through Affect Labeling as Reflected in EEG
articles_hidden.authors: Jinyu Chen; Johanna M.P. Baas; Leon Kenemans; Irene van de Vijver
articles_hidden.abstract: Affect labeling reduces emotional responses during and immediately after use, but evidence for lasting regulatory effects remains mixed. While there is no experiential evidence for lasting effects, psychophysiological studies do hint at a longer-lasting impact. However, neuroimaging research has mainly compared affect labeling with affect matching. Although both involve emotional processing, affect labeling additionally engages linguistic processing. Thus, it remains unclear whether observed neural differences reflect emotion-focused labeling or mere linguistic processing, and whether such effects endure over time. We recorded EEG to examine the effects of affect labeling on negative emotion across two re-exposure phases: immediate and after a short interval (15 minutes). Affect labeling (emotion-specific words) was compared with affect matching (emotion-focused perceptual processing) and feature labeling (linguistic processing without emotional content), allowing us to dissociate emotional and linguistic components. Event-related potentials and EEG oscillatory activity were analyzed in both phases, with pre-intervention neural responses included as baseline. Robust emotion-related neural activity was observed. Negative (vs. neutral) stimuli elicited increased late positive potential (LPP) amplitudes, enhanced fronto-central-parietal theta power, and greater right-hemispheric alpha activity. However, LPP, theta-, and alpha-band power did not show effects of affect labeling compared to the control conditions. Thus, the present findings provide no evidence for a lasting labeling effect. Because we focused on re-exposure, we may have missed potential regulatory effects during the intervention itself. Future research should further identify factors that influence the effectiveness of labeling and clarify when this implicit emotion regulation pathway is engaged.

articles_hidden.title: Human-like social performance does not imply human-like preference inference in large language models
articles_hidden.authors: Mrugsen Gopnarayan; Liis Harjo; Jaan Aru; Sebastian Gluth
articles_hidden.abstract:
As large language models (LLMs) increasingly act on people’s behalf, good decisions may not
indicate accurate inference of human preferences. Across three social inference tasks, we show
that decision quality and preference inference can dissociate. In a multi-attribute bargaining
task, LLMs learned from interaction and often selected offers scoring higher according to buyers’
preferences than human sellers’ offers. However, they inferred preferences less accurately. Models
selectively used behavioral evidence: they exploited previous choices and information about
visual attention, whereas their use of response times was weak and inconsistent compared
to humans. This limitation recurred in classical bargaining and the dictator game, despite
differences in goals and interaction structure. These findings show that higher task scores can
mask differences in how humans and LLMs infer preferences. Hence, evaluations of artificial
social cognition must examine not only what models decide, but what they learn about people
and which behavioral signals they use.

articles_hidden.title: Relations as an organising factor in memory
articles_hidden.authors: Fengyun Hou; Nina Kazanina
articles_hidden.abstract: A well-established finding in memory research is that well-formed verbal input, such as sentences, is better remembered than random word lists, a phenomenon known as the Sentence Superiority Effect (SSE). Whereas the contribution of syntactic well-formedness to the SSE has been widely acknowledged, the present study proposes that semantic relations expressed within sentences or phrases provide an additional contribution to this memory advantage. Across four experiments in English and Chinese, we constructed phrases linking two nouns through a spatial relation (e.g. “a fox on a stump”, Experiments 1-2) or a possessive relation (e.g. “fox’s bag”, Experiments 3-4), and compared them with wordpairs lacking such relations (e.g. “a fox, a stump”, Experiments 1-2; “fox, bag”, Experiments 3-4). Participants listened to sequences of phrases or wordpairs and performed a written free recall task immediately or after a delay. Across experiments, participants were significantly more likely to recall both nouns from the same phrase adjacently in the Phrase condition than in the Wordpair condition. These findings provide robust evidence that semantic relations combine individual concepts into larger memory constructs, underscoring the critical role of relations in organising (verbal) information in memory.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Points and Stories: Gamification That Motivates From Within
articles_hidden.authors: Mahalia Prater Prater Fahey; Ingrid Martin; Toby Wise
articles_hidden.abstract:
Assessments of behaviour and cognition perform best when participants are motivated and
engaged. Since games are inherently engaging and fun, researchers have turned to
“gamification” aiming to make tasks more engaging by incorporating elements of games. Here,
we review influential attempts to gamify behavioural assessments and posit that gamification
can further enhance engagement by taking advantage of a key quality of games: their appeal to
intrinsic motivation. By focusing on the characteristics of games that foster intrinsic motivation,
engagement should follow naturally. Thus, when properly employed, gamification can transform
an uninteresting task that requires extensive training into a short, intuitive game that participants
play willingly. In doing so, we can reveal behavioral profiles that were previously inaccessible
through tasks that are not intrinsically motivating. We also consider how gamification may be at
odds with the goal of enhancing naturalism, and how the goals of enhancing both engagement
and naturalism may align. By keeping both goals in mind, however, ongoing research can aim to
fill a tantalising gap where naturalistic and gamified approaches overlap.

articles_hidden.title: Adapting Non-Violent Resistance for Families of Young People with Complex Neurodevelopmental Needs: A Service Evaluation of Feasibility, Acceptability, and Preliminary Clinical Outcomes
articles_hidden.authors: Alkistis Saramandi; Kirsty Muldoon; Lucy Brett-Taylor
