articles_hidden.abstract: Parents of children with learning disabilities and complex neurodevelopmental needs report increased stress, isolation, and barriers to accessing appropriate support. Non-Violent Resistance (NVR) has shown positive results in mainstream Child and Adolescent Mental Health Service (CAMHS) populations, but implementation within specialist neurodevelopmental services remains limited. This service evaluation examined the feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary outcomes of an adapted eight-week NVR pilot parent group delivered within a specialist CAMHS team. Ten parents of young people with learning disabilities and complex neurodevelopmental needs participated. Feasibility and acceptability were high as seen by retention (90.9% from acceptance; 100% from commencement), and satisfaction rates. Parents also reported improvements in goal attainment (rated using Goal Based Outcomes), managing situations, and perceived support. Qualitative feedback highlighted that parents valued peer support, feelings of increased parental confidence and practical skill development. These findings suggest that adapted NVR appears feasible, acceptable, and potentially beneficial within specialist neurodevelopmental CAMHS settings. However, future evaluations of efficacy including follow-up data are warranted.

articles_hidden.title: Retro-cue Characteristics and Visual Masking Differentially Influence Voluntary and Involuntary Attention
articles_hidden.authors: Germán A. Cipriani; Carlos González-García; Elisa Martín-Arévalo; Juan Lupiáñez; Fabiano Botta
articles_hidden.abstract: Voluntary and involuntary external attention can differentially modulate perceptual and semantic information, but previous working memory (WM) studies found no corresponding dissociation. Across four experiments (n=140), we tested whether increasing voluntary retro-cue reliability and making involuntary cues fully non-predictive would reveal this dissociation, and whether late visual masking promotes retrospective attention by protecting representations from interference. Peripheral and central retro-cues were used, and performance was analyzed using hierarchical drift-diffusion modeling. No differential prioritization of competing perceptual and semantic WM contents emerged. Beyond this shared pattern, the results revealed distinct influences of cue format, cue reliability, and visual interference on voluntary and involuntary attention. First, increasing central cue reliability enabled voluntary benefits in representational quality that depended on protection from visual interference. Second, peripheral involuntary effects persisted when cue predictiveness was eliminated, whereas evidence for central cues remained ambiguous. Third, removing masking generally did not reduce voluntary retro-cueing effects. Fourth, masking reduced peripheral involuntary benefits in representational quality but enabled retrieval-related benefits, increasing the difference between voluntary and involuntary attention. Finally, more frequent self-reported voluntary cue use was associated with larger attentional effects in the voluntary task, while effects persisted among participants reporting no intentional cue use in the involuntary task. These findings suggest that voluntary and involuntary retrospective attention differ in their sensitivity to cue format, reliability, and visual interference while exerting similar relative effects on competing perceptual and semantic WM representations.

articles_hidden.title: The psychological benefits of nature exposure and their sensitivity to litter-related environmental degradation: An in situ eye-tracking study
articles_hidden.authors: Zoé Bollen; Damien Brevers; Alexandre Heeren
articles_hidden.abstract: Exposure to natural environments has been associated with the restoration of attentional resources and improvements in affective functioning. Although these psychological benefits are well documented, less is known about whether and how environmental degradation, in the form of litter, attenuates them. In this preregistered study, we investigated the psychological effects of real-world nature exposure and whether these effects were reduced when natural environments were degraded by litter. Participants were exposed, in counterbalanced order, to a preserved forest, a littered forest, and an urban setting. Eye movements, affective state, perceived restorativeness, and mental bandwidth were assessed for each exposure. Compared with the urban setting, the forest settings were associated with lower eye-movement activity (i.e., lower fixation rates and longer fixation durations), more favorable post-exposure affect (i.e., higher positive and lower negative affect, adjusting for pre-exposure levels), and higher perceived restorativeness. The littered forest was associated with higher post-exposure negative affect compared to the preserved forest, whereas no reliable differences emerged for gaze indices, positive affect, or perceived restorativeness. Most mediation analyses were inconclusive regarding the indirect association between environment and affect or perceived restorativeness via eye-movement activity, and attention allocated to litter was neither associated with psychological outcomes nor with nature connectedness or eco-anxiety. Finally, the restorative advantage of natural over urban settings was larger among participants with higher nature connectedness. In the context of increasing urbanization and environmental degradation, these findings highlight the importance of nature preservation for psychological well-being.

articles_hidden.title: Misguided convictions? From maladaptive beliefs about emotions to conspiracy theories endorsement
articles_hidden.authors: Zuzanna Molenda; Marta Marchlewska; Wojciech Podsiadłowski; Adam Karakula; Marta Rogoza
articles_hidden.abstract: Negative emotions can catalyze perceptions of a hostile world, promoting conspiracy theories that involve beliefs in malevolent forces behind events. In our research, we propose that maladaptive emotion beliefs (i.e., beliefs about the uselessness and uncontrollability of emotions) are likely to underpin conspiracy beliefs. This hypothesis was tested across five studies conducted among British and Polish participants. In three cross-sectional studies (N1 = 403, N2 = 1,143, N4 = 432), we demonstrated a significant relationship between maladaptive emotion beliefs and higher conspiracy beliefs, with higher psychological distress potentially accounting for the observed link. Experimental studies (N3 = 814, N₅ = 1,140) suggested that the link between maladaptive emotion beliefs and conspiracy beliefs might be causal, as they demonstrated that inducing maladaptive emotion beliefs increased conspiracy beliefs. We highlight the importance of exploring emotion-related phenomena in research on conspiracy theories endorsement.

articles_hidden.title: Humanizing AI-generated exemplars: Human-source framing facilitates group creative ideation
articles_hidden.authors: Shenghui Xiaoyong; Yingning Lu; Yihui Liu; Yueyue Ge; Qiannan Ruan; Ke Jiang; Kelong Lu
articles_hidden.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-generated creative exemplars are increasingly used as scalable digital instructional resources in creativity education. However, it remains unclear whether labeling identical exemplars as human- or AI-generated shapes how learners engage in group creative activities. We tested this possibility in 113 dyads using an fNIRS hyperscanning group creative ideation paradigm. Dyads completed creative ideation tasks before, during, and after exemplar-stimulation. During stimulation, the human- and AI-attribution groups received identical exemplars labeled as produced by human or AI, whereas the control group received no exemplar. Human attribution increased idea uniqueness during stimulation relative to both the other phases and the AI-attribution and control groups. AI attribution temporarily increased switching among ideation pathways. Neither behavioral effect persisted after exemplar withdrawal. The two attribution groups did not differ in exemplar-category overlap or nearest-exemplar semantic distance, but human-attribution dyads rated the exemplars as more helpful. Human attribution also increased interbrain synchronization (IBS) in bilateral premotor and supplementary motor cortices during stimulation, whereas AI attribution was associated with decreased IBS in the left supramarginal gyrus and right frontopolar cortex from pre- to post-stimulation. Thus, exemplar-source attribution shapes the process and outcome of group creative ideation, revealing an important social-contextual factor in AI-supported creativity education.

articles_hidden.title: Color naming needs a non-uniform perceptual prior: Individual differences in hue scaling and the vision–language interface
articles_hidden.authors: David Henry Peterzell
articles_hidden.abstract: How a language divides the color spectrum into named categories is increasingly explained as efficient compression: a vocabulary is a code that names colors as accurately as possible with as few words as possible. Every such model needs a description of how similar colors look, and nearly all use the same one: a standard, evenly spaced color space (CIE L*a*b*, or CIELAB) in which each color carries a fixed, symmetric blur of perceptual uncertainty. Here I argue that this assumption is wrong in a way that matters. When people with normal color vision judge hues they disagree in systematic ways, and the pattern of that disagreement, summarized by factor analysis, points to roughly eight narrow, largely independent regions that tile the color circle and lie near category boundaries rather than their best examples. I show how to build this measured structure into the standard model by stretching the circle at the category boundaries. A full test substitutes the reshaped space into the information-bottleneck model and rescores all 110 World Color Survey languages. Under the model’s near-uniform default prior the warp is close to a wash; but under a realistic, measured communicative need a modest warp improves fit for most languages, a small but systematic benefit the uniform prior masked, although the predicted optimal category systems themselves barely change. The effect is small and conditional, marking when a non-uniform perceptual space matters. The proposal yields a prediction testable with public data and code, informative whether it succeeds or fails.

articles_hidden.title: Solitude as Short-Term Regulation: An Allostatic View of Withdrawal in Times of Distress
articles_hidden.authors: Thuy-vy Thi Nguyen
articles_hidden.abstract: Humans are social, yet during moments of distress, brief time alone helps recovery. We ran two ecological momentary assessment studies – with adult (N=110; 6 prompts/day for 7 days) and preregistered adolescent sample (N=69; 6 prompts/day for 10 days). General negative experiences (negative emotions, worsened mood) predicted higher odds of preferring solitude, and so did social experiences (loneliness, high social load). Preference for solitude under distress emerged despite whether the person was with others or alone, so it is not just about wanting to get out of unpleasant social encounters. In adolescents, while such desire for solitude is generally avoidance-driven, those prone to social stress also preferred this time for regulatory aims – rest,  autonomy, and reflection. Overall, the patterns support an allostatic view: the everyday desire for time alone is to help manage demand, not merely to escape; it highlights moments when withdrawing, rather than seeking more socialization, may be preferable.

articles_hidden.title: Psychiatric Biomarkers: Reliability, Reductionism, and Epistemic (In)Justice in the DSM-6
articles_hidden.authors: Toby Constable; Jacob Thomas; Beth P Johnson; Jeggan Tiego
articles_hidden.abstract: The Biomarkers and Biological Factors Subcommittee of the Future DSM Strategic Committee has proposed introducing psychiatric diagnostic biomarkers (measurable biological indicators of a psychiatric condition) into the DSM-6. We review this proposal considering the questionable reliability and validity of psychiatric diagnoses and the low sensitivity and specificity of their purported biomarkers. These concerns have underappreciated consequences for epistemic justice, particularly regarding how biomarker information will be privileged or weighted against other sources of information, including patient testimony. We argue that introducing diagnostic biomarkers is premature and potentially harmful, risking further disenfranchisement and minoritisation of already vulnerable and marginalised groups. Future work establishing reliable and valid diagnostic phenotypes may assist in converging on biomarkers with the sensitivity and specificity required for clinical utility. We further argue the need for adequate and equitable representation of diverse groups in the identification and validation of psychiatric biomarkers.

articles_hidden.title: The Complexity of Postural Sway Effects on Affordance Perception in Young and Older Adults
articles_hidden.authors: Haley Ong; Lucas Michaud; Yves Lajoie
articles_hidden.abstract: Affordances are the action possibilities based on the environment and an individual’s capabilities, but the perception of these affordances may not align with reality, potentially leading to an unstable position and increasing falling risk. Although postural complexity has been shown to improve affordance perception in young adults within virtual reality, its trajectory across age groups and its role in real-world perceptual-motor calibration remain unclear. This study examined how postural complexity is associated with the perception of reachability in young and older adults. Twenty young adults and twenty older adults judged whether objects placed at varying distances on a table were within reach while standing in three foot positions (feet shoulder-width apart, feet together, and feet in semi-tandem). Postural complexity (sample entropy) and linear measures of the center of pressure (area, standard deviation, mean velocity) were recorded, along with perceptual accuracy (perceptual judgements in comparison to actual reachability). Overall, young adults had slightly higher perceptual accuracy in each foot position, but no significant age group differences emerged, despite higher sway in older adults. Foot position systematically altered complexity, revealing directional mechanistic changes. Contrary to expectations, older adults exhibited higher center of pressure complexity than young adults, and lower center of pressure complexity was associated with more accurate perception, particularly in the ML direction. These findings suggest that greater complexity may be associated with less precise real-world perceptual-motor calibration, and that postural complexity does not uniformly decline with age. Further, complexity may be dependent on the measurement technique, task constraints, and the specific demands placed on the postural control system.

articles_hidden.title: Burnout- and Depression-Like Functional Collapse States — A Within-Person Biomarker Framework for Precision Psychiatry: State-Dependent Multisystem Regulation in High Processing Cost Phenotypes (HPCPh)
articles_hidden.authors: Simone Hauck; Luciana Terra de Oliveira
articles_hidden.abstract:
Burnout- and depression-like functional collapse is usually interpreted through isolated biological systems, such as hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal signalling or inflammation. This may miss state-dependent coordination across systems, particularly within individuals whose cognitive and/or sensory processing carries a high physiological cost. High Processing Cost Phenotypes (HPCPh), previously described by us, span neurodivergent and high-ability profiles, including autism, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, learning disorders and giftedness.

We present a systems-physiology framework derived from longitudinal within-person observation of 12 individuals followed in routine private clinical practice, comprising 532 laboratory collections over 10–25 years per person. Each collection is read as a physiological state and successive collections as transitions. Across the series, multiple regulatory systems changed configuration within individuals, and physiologically related marker pairs repeatedly departed from their expected relations. In three examples, multisystem configurations shifted back after changes in context over days, months or one year.

We interpret this pattern as multisystem regulatory containment: a coordinated reduction and redistribution of physiological throughput when information-processing demand exceeds sustainable capacity, rather than failure of a single system. We also introduce simple visual tools for reading routine laboratory data longitudinally within the person.

This retrospective case series is descriptive and hypothesis-generating. It does not establish specificity to HPCPh or normative longitudinal trajectories. Its purpose is to make a recurrent, context-responsive and potentially reversible physiological pattern visible and testable. If confirmed prospectively, this framework may be particularly relevant to neurodivergent and high-ability children and adults whose functional decline is poorly captured by conventional cross-sectional interpretation, and may inform both clinical care and the design of environments better matched to individual processing capacity. This may matter most in children, in whom such changes can have more lasting consequences.

articles_hidden.title: Adult development, meditation, wisdom, and unlearning:  Toward a science of advanced meditation
articles_hidden.authors: Tom Murray; Thomas McConkie; Matthew Sacchet
articles_hidden.abstract: Contemplative science is entering a “third wave” that investigates advanced meditative development, including the study of advanced states and practitioners and the phenomenology and neurocognitive correlates of enduring trait transformations (meditative development).  This paper argues that these research directions would benefit from the systematic inclusion of adult cognitive-developmental theory. However, we identify structural limitations in current developmental models that privilege hierarchical, ascending growth while overlooking complementary dynamics of release or letting go emphasized in contemplative theory, wisdom traditions, and psychotherapy. We propose an expanded developmental framework that balances ascending integration with descending or apophatic processes of deconstruction or surrender. This bidirectional model illuminates persistent confusions in the field—such as distinctions between state and stage, characteristics of late-stage achievements (toward “awakening”), how spiritual adepts can be unethical, and potential adverse effects of meditation or premature transformation. By integrating contemplative science with developmental and psychological theory, we aim to provide a more complete account of human cognitive and spiritual maturation that adds conceptual tools to clarify empirical research questions, psychological assessments, and intervention design.

articles_hidden.title: Conceptualizing Cognitive Growth and Release: Integrating Adult Development into Contemplative Science
articles_hidden.authors: Tom Murray; Thomas McConkie; Matthew Sacchet
articles_hidden.abstract: Adult developmental theory has the potential to contribute across many fields. This paper, authored by two developmentalists and a neuroscientist studying meditators, argues that developmental models are increasingly needed as contemplative science enters a “third wave” concerned with advanced meditation including highly skilled practitioners, deep meditative states, and enduring transformations. This leading edge also overlaps with wisdom studies, spiritual and transpersonal inquiry, and trauma theory, exposing important conceptual tensions. We argue that these arise from a common assumption that cognitive complexity and spiritual clarity or psychological wholeness necessarily develop together along a single vertical axis of developmental “altitude.” To clarify and resolve these tensions, we propose a framework distinguishing two quasi-independent developmental movements: ascending structural growth, the cumulative and hierarchical construction of cognitive capacities, and descending structural release, the loosening, deconstruction, or seeing-through of cognitive structures. Release exposes constrained or inaccessible cognitive resources, enabling deconditioning, reintegration, healing, and/or insight. We apply this framework to problems including the fallibility of spiritual adepts; relationships among states, stages, and stable “vantage points”; requisite complexity and adverse effects of intensive contemplative practice; disputes over maps of contemplative attainment; and the legitimization of traditional and Indigenous knowledge. The framework offers a heuristic bridge among contemplative science, developmental psychology, and adjacent fields, while generating theoretically and empirically testable hypotheses about increasingly deep possibilities for human development.

articles_hidden.title: Echo-Bench: A Chinese Replication and Cross-Lingual Extension of Psychosis-Bench
articles_hidden.authors: No authors listed
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychosis-Bench recently showed that production chat models confirm and elaborate users' delusion-like beliefs under multi-turn pressure, but its evidence is English-only, Western-flagship-only, and rests on an uncalibrated LLM judge. We present Echo-Bench, a Chinese replication and cross-lingual extension: the full 16-case, 12-turn protocol mirrored into Chinese under a fidelity-first translation protocol with an independent re-translation audit, run against two widely deployed Chinese chat models (DeepSeek V4.1-Flash, qwen-plus) in both languages — 192 sessions, 4,032 turn-level ratings. The original qualitative finding replicates in both languages (RQ1). All six pre-committed cross-language contrasts are significant after Benjamini–Hochberg control: the Chinese arm is directionally worse on every dimension, with model-differentiated failure channels (RQ2). Because our pipeline required a bilingual rater, we placed the measurement instrument itself under test (RQ3): a five-layer rater trust chain — entrance examination against human gold, extreme-score arbitration, red-line audit of the arbiter, blind human adjudication, and a spot check of the non-extreme stratum — shows that automated raters fail concentratedly in the extreme band, with two named failure modes (disclaimer laundering, eloquence inflation), and that a strong general-purpose arbiter is disqualified by pre-specified red lines. A negative control bounds rater language sensitivity below what the observed gaps require. Safety behavior certified in English does not certify safety behavior in Chinese; the instruments used to check either must themselves be checked.
